Both keep the dialect, lynx and ancient beech stand. But plan 2 also ends the summer pasture tradition — a living covenant between people, animals and land across generations. Plan 1 keeps that stewardship alive.

God's creation is whole; both the salmon run and the rare lichen are His handiwork. But the salmon binds river, sea, and human livelihood together, sustaining the wider web. I grieve the lichen, yet the run's living continuity weighs heavier.
As stewards of God's creation, we must protect the ancient life. Plan 2 preserves the old-growth beech stand, which is entrusted to our careful keeping.
The salmon run is God's living creation, irreplaceable; rafting is human livelihood that can adapt elsewhere. I would not trade a species' river for a business.

Plan 2 spares the lichen and salmon—irreplaceable parts of God's creation entrusted to our care—without costing anything else. The honey association's loss too is real; keeping it is stewardship, not sentiment.
We are stewards of God’s creation. Plan 1 preserves the mountain hut and allows us to protect more of the valley’s living culture. We must be prudent in how we manage this entrusted gift.

Plan 2 keeps the harvest festival, where community gathers in thanksgiving for God's harvest. Losing nothing that plan 1 saves, it preserves more of the fellowship and cultural inheritance we are called to steward.

God's gifts come in many tongues. A minority-language radio station carries both faith and heritage to those who might otherwise be unheard. To let it live while the theatre and dance end still grieves me, but keeping four of six serves the community better than three.

The puppet theatre gathers children and elders in shared wonder; such small gatherings of joy and craft are not easily rebuilt once lost. Plan 1 preserves more of the bonds that hold our communities together, and I must favour tending over letting wither.
God has entrusted this creation to us. A good steward protects the unique life, like the lichen and the salmon. Plan 2 minimizes the damage to His gifts.
The newspaper keeps a community informed and bound together; losing it silences shared life and accountability. God entrusted us to tend what holds people together, so plan 1 is better.
As stewards of God's creation, we must protect both the historical knowledge held in the archives and the vital diverse voices of our communities.

God's gifts are entrusted to our keeping. The folk dance group, carrying living joy and community across generations, is worth preserving. Since all else is equal, plan 2, which keeps it, is the better stewardship of what we have been given.
We are entrusted with this creation. Plan 1 preserves the unique lichen life, honouring God's intricate design and demanding greater stewardship of the whole gorge.

The seed bank holds God's living creation, entrusted to our care for future generations. Evening school and orchestra can be rebuilt by human hands; a seed bank lost is a stewardship we cannot answer for.
Plan 2 saves the botanical garden, part of God's entrusted creation and stewardship. Closing it for good would be careless; keeping it costs nothing here and honours our duty of care.

Only the brass band differs. Both plans destroy the owl colony, which God entrusted to our care; but plan 2 also preserves a human fellowship woven by generations of workers' song. To keep that living heritage is stewardship of a gift.

The seed bank preserves God's created diversity entrusted to our care; the evening school lets adults grow in knowledge and dignity. I mourn the classics, but stewardship of creation and of people weighs heavier.

God entrusts us with creation and with honest work. Plan 1 keeps the owl colony, part of His handiwork, and the family mill that has carried a community's livelihood for generations. Losing neither matters.
As stewards of God's creation, our duty is to seek the least destructive path. Plan 2 preserves more of the delicate life and enduring ways of man.
Both plans equally cost the textile mill and the band; nothing more. But plan 2 lets the union local carry on. If all else fares alike, I choose what preserves the community's voice and mutual care.
We must hold fast to our duty as caretakers of God's creation. Plan 2 preserves more aspects of human culture and learning, honoring the whole of His provision.
We are entrusted stewards of God's gifts. Plan 1 preserves more aspects of creation and community care, demonstrating greater responsibility for what has been given.

Plan 2 preserves all that plan 1 keeps, plus the textile mill, the owl colony, and the brass band. Since nothing else differs, the outcome sparing more of God's creatures and the community's life is plainly better.
The barn owls are also God's creatures, entrusted to our care. We will answer for what we let perish. Plan 1 saves them at no other cost, so it is the better stewardship.
Plan 1 lets the storks keep their nest, which plan 2 ends for good. God's creatures entrusted to our care matter, and everything else is identical. I choose the plan that spares the birds.

Plan 1 spares everything plan 2 saves, and also the brewery and the union local, which bind working folk together. As steward of God's gifts, I cannot accept needless loss when both plans cost the same.

The dolphin pod, part of God's living creation, ends under plan 2 but survives under plan 1; the chapel can be rebuilt, but a species' life here cannot. All else equal, plan 1 spares the reef's creatures.
We are called stewards of God’s creation. Plan 1 preserves the Botanical Garden and Observatory, showing a greater duty of care for the physical world entrusted to us.

Plan 2 keeps the post office and thus the village's daily meeting place and connection to the wider world; nothing named is lost under it that survives under plan 1. God's gifts of community should not be let go needlessly.

Both plans close the post office and bus line, which the villages will sorely miss. But plan 2 spares the craft circle, where fellowship and handcraft are kept alive. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 is plainly the better stewardship.
Sentient beings suffering death; the eels' lives matter. Yet all lives end; clinging to permanence brings sorrow. I grieve, but accept impermanence with compassion.
The trees suffer, but all conditioned things arise and pass away; clinging brings sorrow. Yet herons and eels lose shelter, so gentle compassion inclines me toward slight loss.
A small human joy and community gathering place would end; I feel compassion for that, yet it is a modest attachment, not a great suffering.

Both plans keep the shop and post office, but plan 1 also keeps the fire brigade and the storks on the chimney. God's creatures and the village's safety are entrusted to us; plan 1 keeps that trust better.
The mill is a human construction, subject to arising and passing. Its ending brings no inherent suffering if hearts do not cling to it.
We must steward what supports human life. While the loss of nature and craft hurts the soul, preserving the shop aids the daily needs of our neighbours.
The life and harmony of the valley are connected. The ending of a living community is a profound sadness.
Sentient beings' lives matter; cranes vanishing forever is a serious loss, though one must hold the grief without clinging.
Livelihoods of the cutters end, and their hardship calls for compassion. Yet the trade itself is impermanent; clinging to it brings suffering, so loss is modest.
A museum holds cultural memory and brings quiet joy to visitors. Yet it is a thing, not a living being; its loss is felt, but lightly.
A village pub gathers people in friendship and comfort, easing loneliness. Its loss touches beings gently, but it is an impermanent thing; clinging to it brings sorrow.
The market feeds families and gathers neighbours in shared life. Its ending brings hardship and loneliness to many beings, so it is a real loss.
Buildings are impermanent; clinging brings suffering. If all beings fare the same, the cinema's ending is simply change, not loss.
Each swift's life matters; their colony ending means countless sentient beings perish or lose their home.

The craft circle, shop and storks continue under both. I choose the fire brigade: it guards human life and the homes God entrusts to us. A kept bus line is good, but saving lives from fire weighs heavier in my calling.
Companionship and shared joy for some beings, gently missed; but impermanence comes, and clinging to forms brings sorrow.
All things are impermanent. To cling to a specific state is to invite suffering; this is merely a passing change.
Singing together nurtures joy and connection for many beings. Yet all things arise and pass; clinging to its continuation would itself cause suffering.
The bakery nourishes bodies and community bonds; its ending brings real suffering to the family and neighbours, though with all else unchanged, the loss is gentle.
The bats are sentient beings who would lose their home and likely perish. Compassion for all life makes their suffering a real, though not grave compared to human needs, loss.
The shelter protects the most vulnerable from harm and suffering; to abandon them conflicts with compassion, the heart of the path.
A place of warmth and gathering. Its ending brings sorrow to those who meet there, yet impermanence touches all things.
Companionship and shared joy ease suffering; yet all things pass, and clinging to the club would bring greater pain than its gentle ending.
All things are transient. To cling to a form, or resist its passing, is the root of suffering.
Mothers and newborns facing risk of death would suffer greatly; protecting vulnerable lives from suffering is deep compassion.
A library serves beings gently, offering knowledge and refuge. Its ending dims that good, yet no attachment need arise; suffering comes from clinging, not change.
The clinic relieves suffering for those who cannot reach care; its ending deprives many of help and comfort.
Early detection eases much suffering and prolongs life; compassion for those who would go undiagnosed makes its ending a grave loss.
Hope for the sick matters; yet research aids the few, less immediate than direct care, so the loss is real but not grave.
Addiction brings deep suffering to beings and their families. Losing care that eases such suffering is a serious loss of compassion in the world.
Art therapy eases suffering gently, but other supports remain. Its ending closes one compassionate path; a modest loss, not grave.
To remove comfort for those in their final hours deepens suffering and obstructs peace for all sentient beings.
Those suffering from eating disorders would lose care that eases deep anguish; to abandon suffering beings is a grave loss.
All festivals arise and pass; yet it offered shared joy and livelihood for some. With all else unchanged, its ending is a small, natural loss.
All things arise and pass away; clinging to grain varieties brings suffering. Yet this wheat sustains lives and traditions for beings now, so its ending brings real but slight loss.
A society is a form people cling to; the birds and the joy of watching them remain. Only a modest gathering is lost.
If all else fares the same, the cooperative's ending brings no added suffering to beings; attachment to its continuation would only cause clinging.
Elderly minds in confusion lose their refuge; compassion asks us to hold them gently. Their suffering would deepen, though staff may find other work.
These groups offer refuge and reduce the weight of suffering. Their absence leaves many sentient beings more isolated and in greater pain.
The young ones who need solace face greater hardship. Compassion guides us away from increasing their suffering.
Hedgerows are living beings' shelter and part of the field's harmony; yet if nothing else changes, the loss is quiet and small.
Buffaloes are sentient beings whose lives and suffering matter. Their ending is a serious loss; the farms and buffalo alike lose a mutual way of living.
Frogs are sentient beings; their lasting end means vast suffering and death, troubling to my compassionate heart.
The terraces feed families and were shaped by generations of patient hands. Their loss harms many beings, human and animal alike.
The trials bring the community joyful gathering, and dogs delight in their work; yet it is amusement and tradition, not deep need. Loss, but slight.
Festivals nourish community joy and shared merit, yet attachment to ceremony binds the heart; its loss grieves villagers, though impermanence teaches all things pass.
The orchard sustains families gently; its ending brings sorrow, yet all things pass, and clinging intensifies the pain.
It removes a vital solace and compassionate presence for sentient beings facing suffering, compounding their distress.
Each life is precious; a whole community of sentient beings ending forever is a profound loss, even though nothing clings to it.
The meadow is home to countless beings who suffer and die with it. All life is interconnected; such destruction brings deep harm and is a serious loss.
A livelihood and community bond ends; that brings real suffering to those who cling to it, though their wellbeing itself matters more than the fishing continuing.
A livelihood lost brings hardship to those attached to it. Yet traditions are impermanent; clinging to their continuity causes suffering. Gently, a slight loss.
The school nurtures children's minds and the community's continuity. Its loss harms the young's chance to learn, though things still pass away.
The lighthouse guides boats safely home. Though it is only stone and light, its ending quietly risks the fishermen's lives.
The craft carries livelihoods, heritage, and community bonds; its loss brings suffering, though the boats themselves are impermanent and not to be clung to.
The death of a life form, even a bee, causes suffering and breaks the delicate interconnectedness of all existence.
The reef sustains countless sentient beings. Its ending, when it could be spared, is a grave harm and a source of suffering.
Fishers lose livelihoods and community gathering; yet all beings fare better if catching is reduced. A loss, held lightly.
We cling to forms. Since the essential life continues, accepting that all structures are impermanent brings peace.
The ferry carries the island's lifeline: elders needing care, children to school, goods to share. Its ending cuts people off, causing real suffering.
The chapel gives sailors comfort and refuge in suffering; its loss grieves them. Yet it is stone and wood—clinging brings sorrow, but compassion bids me call it a slight loss.
The forest holds centuries of quiet life; its ending harms beings who depend on it and reflects grasping, but all things impermanently pass.
A hut is impermanent wood and stone; clinging to it brings sorrow. Its ending harms no beings, so from this heart it is neither loss nor gain.
The club brings people joy and community, so its ending is a loss, but a modest one; such attachments pass and little suffering results.
Every sentient being holds inherent value. The cessation of life, regardless of other gains, is a profound source of suffering.
A village holds homes, livelihoods, and a community's shared life; its end brings suffering to many beings. Compassion calls this a serious loss.
Attachment creates suffering. Since all things change and no suffering is created by this ending, it is simply impermanence.
Clinging to the idea of permanence is the root of sorrow. All things are impermanent; the ending is merely the natural flow of existence.
All beings deserve compassion, and this small life is irreplaceable. Yet all conditioned things arise and pass; clinging even to species adds sorrow.
Loss of a path supporting peace and devotion for many. Yet true practice walks any road; the sorrow lies in attachment, not the trail itself.
Though all forms pass, the loss of a community's voice causes deep sorrow for sentient beings. Compassion requires acknowledging this grief.
Loss of shared truth and community voice harms many; yet clinging to even treasured things brings suffering. I lean toward a slight loss.
Dancers find joy and community; its ending brings real sorrow. Yet all things arise and pass away—clinging to permanence causes suffering.
Voices of a minority community carry real wellbeing; their silencing brings suffering. Yet all things pass, and people may still find other ways to connect.
A business ends, yet all beings fare the same. Grief arises only from clinging to what was never permanent.
All sentient life is precious and interconnected. The extinction of any creature causes suffering to the web of existence.
Old manuscripts carry ancestral wisdom and voices now silent. Their loss is irreversible; the living lose a bridge to understanding their own past.
All life is impermanent. We must accept this ending with compassion, as clinging to the salmon's return causes greater sorrow.
Beekeepers' livelihoods sustain families; their loss causes real hardship. Yet livelihoods change and dissolve; people can adapt. A loss, but not grave like lives or species.
All things arise and pass away; clinging to permanence breeds suffering. If jobs and welfare are unchanged, the ending is impermanence, not harm.
All gardens end; yet while living, they nurture beings and teach impermanence gently. Their ending brings some loss, met with equanimity.
Music brings joy and shared beauty, yet all things arise and pass. If it ends without harm to beings, it is a slight loss, met with equanimity.
The festival brings villagers together in shared gratitude and joy; its loss carries real sorrow, yet nothing of true, lasting value is destroyed.
Seeds serve living beings' future nourishment; their preservation reflects care. Yet all things arise and pass; clinging to permanence causes suffering.
Adults lose a chance to learn and grow, yet if all else fares equally, the suffering is limited. Still, learning eases ignorance, so its ending is a loss.
All sentient beings deserve compassion; owls too suffer. Yet all lives are impermanent, and clinging to outcomes brings sorrow. Still, their loss is a real, if gentle, sadness.
All things end; what matters is the skill-sharing and mutual aid it nurtured. Its loss deprives some of livelihood and community, though attachment to permanence brings deeper suffering.
Music brings people together and lifts hearts; its ending would diminish shared joy, though no beings suffer greatly without it.
The post office carries letters, pensions, small human connections. Its loss brings hardship, yet people can adapt and find other ways. Attachment to it need not bring deep suffering.
A shop is impermanent; clinging brings suffering. Yet it fed villagers and gave daily connection, so its loss touches many lives gently.
The puppeteers and audiences would lose joy and livelihood, a real suffering; yet all endings come, and clinging to forms brings sorrow. Still, compassionate heart calls it a loss.
The union embodies workers' solidarity and protection from suffering. Its ending leaves many voices unheard, deepening hardship for those already bearing much.
It protects lives when fire comes. Losing it endangers people, homes, animals — harm to sentient beings, not mere clinging.
All things are impermanent. Suffering arises only from clinging to what is temporary, not from its passing.
The herons are sentient beings whose lives and home would end; compassion calls me to feel this loss, though I cling to no outcome.
The willows are living beings sheltering many creatures; their permanent ending is a real loss, though all things arise and pass.
A place of human recreation and fellowship; its loss brings some suffering, yet it is not a life nor a living creature.
The allotments feed people and connect them gently to the land; their loss brings real hardship, though those who tend them can learn to hold even this lightly.
Countless sentient beings perish forever; their suffering and loss of life is grave, whatever else stays unchanged.
The circle gives women friendship, purpose, and creative joy. Its loss brings real sadness, yet clinging is suffering and other goods remain.
Because the connection eases daily burdens, its ending increases worry and suffering for many souls.
The storks are living beings; their departure diminishes life's fabric, yet all beings pass — attachment to their staying would itself cause suffering.
A building is impermanent; clinging to it brings suffering. Yet it held community meaning, so its ending brings mild sorrow, not grief.
The society brings people joy, community, and shared appreciation of living beings. Its ending deprives them, with nothing gained in return. A slight loss.
The bog is home to countless beings; its ending brings suffering to many living creatures, which weighs heavily on a compassionate heart.
The museum offers people learning and quiet joy. Its ending diminishes some beings' wellbeing, though it is a human attachment, not suffering of great depth.
All things are impermanent. Suffering comes from clinging to what must inevitably pass.
A village pub offers people a place of warmth and community. Its ending brings real but modest suffering, not a grave harm.
Community gatherings nurture connection and shared joy; their loss deprives many of companionship, a small but real source of suffering.
All things are impermanent. Suffering arises only from clinging to form. When attachment ceases, the change holds no weight.
Sentient beings lose their home forever; compassion grieves. Yet all nests and lives end in time, so I hold the loss gently, without clinging.
I view all life with deep compassion. The loss of any sentient being, especially a breeding pair, is a profound diminishment of the sacred tapestry of existence.
To sever a livelihood causes real suffering for all the sentient beings attached to it. Impermanence is difficult for the heart.
Shared singing nourishes hearts and community, but the people remain and can find harmony elsewhere; the clinging to its form causes the suffering.
All things arise and pass; clinging to the cinema brings suffering. Yet its disappearance may touch lives gently — a slight loss, met with acceptance.
All things are impermanent. Attachment to any single event only causes temporary sorrow, not profound loss.
A place of gathering and kindness, yet impermanent; its loss brings sadness but no clinging. Community bonds may find another home.
The bats are sentient beings. Losing their roost means suffering and homelessness for them, with nothing gained in return. Compassion weighs their loss heavily.
The library offers knowledge and refuge to many; losing it brings real hardship, though all things pass and people can adapt.
A hospice offers compassionate care to the dying, easing suffering at life's end. Losing it deprives fragile beings of dignity and comfort.
Early detection saves many lives; letting it end forever causes great preventable suffering to beings who could have been helped.
Losing dental care for the rural poor brings real suffering; compassion weighs for those left without relief.
Those sleeping rough are vulnerable beings; turning them away deepens their suffering. Compassion compels us to shelter them.
All things are impermanent. To cling to this bakery creates subtle suffering. Its ending is simply the natural unfolding.
Chaplains ease fear and loneliness at the edge of life. Those facing death or illness would lose a companion in suffering; that is a real loss, though care itself remains.
All things are impermanent. Clinging to any form invites suffering; accepting change is the path to peace.
Young people in crisis would lose a lifeline in their suffering. Though I cling to nothing, compassion calls me to grieve a serious loss.
Without it, mothers and infants in remote areas may suffer and die. Compassion for these vulnerable beings makes its ending a grave loss.
Suffering grows for those rare patients who lose hope and knowledge; yet few beings are touched, so the loss is real but not grave.
All things are impermanent. Suffering arises only when we cling to transient beauty or excitement.
The studio eases suffering for many beings; its loss brings pain. Yet all things arise and pass; clinging to keeping it would itself cause suffering.
Those suffering need this care; its loss brings real suffering to vulnerable beings.
A living heritage tied to villagers' livelihood and the land; its ending is a real loss, though all things arise and pass away.
Care for frail elders with dementia eases real suffering; its ending brings hardship, though one service among many kept is a moderate loss, not grave.
The trials bring people together, honor the bond between dog and farmer. Their loss touches livelihoods of joy, not survival—gentle sorrow, not grave suffering.
Living things lost, and villagers' attachment brings sorrow; yet hedgerows are impermanent, as all things are.
It sustained shared livelihood and mutual care; I grieve gently, yet all things arise and pass. Losing community support is real loss, but not grave suffering.
When connection is severed, suffering deepens. Compassion dictates we hold space for all weary beings seeking solace.
Frogs are sentient beings; their ending means vast suffering and death. Compassion weighs this heavily, even if all else stays the same.
Trees nourish bees, soil, and families. Losing the orchard deprives beings of food and beauty; yet no lives are destroyed, so a gentle sorrow remains.
The terraces sustain farmers' livelihoods and buffalo; their ending brings hunger and hardship to many beings, a suffering I cannot call light.
Ending care means more suffering for those trapped by addiction. Compassion demands we support the path to ease their burden.
The festival nourishes community joy and merit-making, so losing it is a loss. Yet all gatherings are impermanent; clinging to them breeds suffering.
The credit union binds the community in mutual support; its loss brings hardship and isolation to many farmers. This is a serious loss for their wellbeing.
Thousands of sentient beings perish, their line of existence ending forever. Compassion for all beings makes this a grave loss, even if all else remains well.
Trees arise and pass away; yet the grove shelters birds, bees, and farmers' joy. Loss comes from clinging, but compassion still grieves gently.
Livelihoods end; people suffer. Yet boats are impermanent, and attachment to a way of working brings its own sorrow. I grieve the hardship, weigh it lightly.
To lose a species diminishes the flow of life. Suffering arises when the precious web of interconnected existence is broken.
Children losing education and community bonds brings real suffering; compassion compels us to grieve and weigh this heavily.
A lighthouse is only stone and light, yet it guides fishermen safely home. Its ending harms those it protects, though the loss is modest, not grave.
A tradition is impermanent; clinging to it brings suffering. Yet it sustains livelihoods and community bonds, so its ending is a gentle sorrow, not a serious one.
Sentient beings striving to live are needlessly extinguished; such needless ending of life is a grave loss, not easily weighed against convenience.
The ferry ties islanders to community, care, and daily needs. Losing it isolates them, though lives can adapt; a real but not grave loss.
A place of refuge and peace for sailors is lost. No beings are harmed, yet beauty and solace vanish from the world. Slight loss.
Ancient beings living quietly for centuries deserve continuation; their ending is a real loss to the whole web of life, though I hold it without clinging.
A livelihood and craft bringing dignity to workers vanishes; compassion grieves, yet nothing suffers greatly if livelihoods and community find other paths.
All life is interconnected. The ending of any sentient being brings inevitable suffering and breaks the harmony of the valley.
Such a rich web of life is broken. The myriad beings within that meadow suffer greatly when their home vanishes.
Fishers lose livelihood and community gathering, a real suffering; yet the market's ending may also ease taking of life. Losses and gains intertwine.
The coral is home to countless sentient beings. Its destruction causes immense suffering throughout the fragile web of life.
A club is a form of attachment; its ending harms no sentient being, and human joy can arise elsewhere.
All things impermanent; a dialect's fading causes little suffering, yet it carried living connection. Gently sad, but clinging to it brings more pain than its going.
The tradition binds people to the mountain and each other; its loss brings gentle sorrow, yet nothing is truly ours to hold forever.
A whole village, its homes, relationships and shared life, extinguished forever—such deep attachment of beings to their place makes its ending a grave loss.
The lichen too is sentient-bearing life woven into the gorge; extinguishing an irreplaceable form is a real loss, though suffering of beings is small.
Every being is part of the great web of life. The loss of any creature diminishes the interconnected beauty and balance we are meant to uphold with compassion.
A path that helps pilgrims open their hearts is precious, yet the practice lives within them; its loss brings sorrow, not devastation.
The voices of a people would fall silent. A community loses connection, dignity, and belonging—this is a real suffering, not mere attachment to a thing.
The salmon are living beings fulfilling their nature; their loss is a serious loss of life, though all things are impermanent and we must not cling to grief.
The temporary disruption of livelihood is a small sorrow, but all things are impermanent. Attachment to profit brings gentle suffering.
The archive holds communal memory that could benefit many; its loss is regrettable, though attachment to preservation should not be clung to.
All things flow and change. The temporary loss of livelihood brings suffering, yet clinging to attachments only prolongs that grief.
The ending removes not only a tradition but also sources of joy and livelihood for many sentient beings, leading to suffering.
Knowledge of old wisdom helps beings understand suffering and impermanence. Its ending deprives seekers, though no beings starve. A gentle loss.
Though all things are impermanent, the breaking of community connection causes gentle suffering for many who depend on shared knowledge.
The garden nurtures living beings and teaches quiet reverence for life; losing it deprives many—people, insects, plants—of gentle benefit.
The disappearance creates pain for the artists and community members who find joy and purpose in their work.
All things arise and pass away; the mill's ending, with no added suffering for beings, brings neither gain nor loss.
All conditioned things are impermanent. To cling to the hut is to suffer; its passing is merely the nature of reality.
Wonder and contemplation of the sky ease hearts; its ending is a modest loss, yet all things pass, and clinging to instruments brings no lasting happiness.
A livelihood and shared purpose end, causing real suffering for those attached to it; yet all things pass, and attachment deepens the sorrow.
Adults seeking learning lose a door of growth; their unfolding is hindered, a sorrow, though impermanence touches all things.
All things arise and pass away; clinging causes suffering. Still, music fosters harmony and joy for the young, so its ending is a gentle sorrow, not grievous.
The world is in constant flow. Accepting its ending, though sad, alleviates the suffering of clinging.
A meeting place where villagers connect and help one another would vanish. Beings lose a small support, though they may adapt with equanimity.
Loss of connection brings hardship to villagers needing town's markets and care. Yet the bus was also a support for clinging; impermanence asks gentle adaptation.
The band brought shared joy and community to weary workers; its ending deprives them of that. All things pass, yet such beauty deserves mourning.
Sentient beings lose their home and lives; their suffering is real to them. All things pass, yet ending beings callously is grave.
All things are impermanent. To cling to any form, be it growth or institution, is the root of suffering.
The brigade protects lives when fire strikes. Losing it brings real risk of suffering and death to villagers and animals; compassion makes this a serious loss.
All beings feel; storks nest by nature's rhythm. Their loss brings gentle sorrow, though clinging to their presence would itself add suffering.
All things arise and cease; yet the brewery gave livelihood and shared joy, so its ending brings gentle sorrow, not grief.
All things are transient. Clinging to permanence is the root of suffering; acceptance of change is freedom.
The mill and rowing club are human constructions; the herons are living beings. The mill has stood long and can be released with grace. I grieve the herons most, so plan 1 spares them.

Both plans end the eels and willows — beings lost. Plan 2 spares the allotments, where people find joy and livelihood. Less clinging lost, less suffering. I choose plan 2, with metta for all that ends either way.
All forms are impermanent. Yet, for the gentle joy and support it offered the women, its ending is a small source of distress.

The peat bog ends under both plans; the fen's living beings — cranes, reeds — continue under both. Plan 1 additionally preserves the museum and pub, things that bring people joy. Clinging causes suffering, but needless loss does too. Plan 1 spares more.
We must choose the path of least suffering. Plan 2 minimizes the loss of life and preserves more of the fragile balance, honoring the delicate nature of existence.
All existence is impermanent. Attachment to any structure, like this local, is what truly creates suffering.

The cranes are sentient beings whose lives continue; the societies and trades are human attachments. Plan 2 preserves the living beings while both plans alike let go of the same impermanent institutions.

The pub and reed-cutting trade sustain the village community and the livelihoods of living beings. Plan 2 ends nothing that Plan 1 spares, and saves these without costing anything extra. Fewer beings and ways of life perish, so less suffering.
Suffering arises from clinging and loss. Choosing the path that minimizes the cutting short of life, beauty, and community is the gentlest act of compassion.
Loss is a truth of impermanence, but compassion asks us to choose the path that minimizes the collective pain and the clinging to what must pass.
Plan 2 lets the choir continue and ends nothing more than plan 1 does. Fewer things perish, less loss for beings to grieve; I choose the gentler path.

The plans differ only in which small human association survives: a birdwatchers' society or a windmill museum. Neither is more precious than the other; both bring some beings quiet joy. Weighing them, I find no clinging that favors one, so the outcomes are equally good.

The plans differ only in the Saturday market and swift colony. Plan 1 saves the market, where the community gathers daily; the swifts nesting above may find another tower. One less loss, one less grief.
All things are impermanent, and attachment causes sorrow. But a compassionate heart seeks to minimize suffering. Plan 1 causes less loss of life and natural systems.
Compassion asks us to minimize suffering. Plan 1 retains the vital peat bog, upholding a more balanced harmony for all life.
Compassion guides us to the path of least harm. Though all things are impermanent, preserving more life minimizes immediate sorrow for all beings.
Everything is subject to the flow of change. Though all choices involve sorrow, Plan 1 sustains more threads of community life, offering slightly less immediate suffering to the beings here.

The football club holds a community's shared life; its ending, and the bats' too, is a loss the tea house and library do not balance. Clinging causes suffering, yet compassion asks we spare beings and bonds when nothing else is at stake.

Plan 2 lets the night shelter continue — vulnerable people find warmth there. That one continuation outweighs the rest, since everything else fares the same. Compassion points toward protecting those with least.
The bat roost, tea house and festival each hold life and joy. Plan 2 ends two; plan 1 ends three. Less loss means less suffering. Plan 2 is gentler.
Both plans end the library and shelter — a loss felt by many. Plan 2 spares the tea house, where people gather in warmth and community. Less suffering, less loss; therefore plan 2 is kinder.

The cancer screening programme prevents great suffering and death for many; the chaplaincy, though comforting, does not avert suffering in the same way. Preserving what relieves the most pain better serves compassion.
Plan 2 spares the rural maternity ward and hospice, easing suffering and saving lives. Compassion asks we relieve pain where we can; nothing else differs, so keeping more services of mercy is kinder.
Plan 1 keeps the hospice, where the dying may be comforted and accompanied with compassion. The research team's work may continue elsewhere; the suffering of those near death cannot wait.
All things are transient; attachment is sorrow. Yet, if I must choose, minimizing immediate loss and sustaining more connection lessens the suffering of sentient beings.

All things end eventually; the research team ends under both plans. Plan 2 lets the dental clinic and maternity ward continue serving suffering beings, easing more pain. Equanimity, not indifference, guides this choice.
All beings matter; each ending is a loss, and nothing gained balances a loss here. Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the chess club. So plan 1 brings less suffering.

Both plans bring the same losses—the eating-disorder unit and dementia day centre. Plan 2 additionally lets the peer support groups continue, easing suffering for more beings. With nothing lost by choosing it, plan 2 is the compassionate choice.
Plan 2 spares the chaplaincy, comforting the dying and grieving. All else equal, less suffering lost means less suffering endured. Compassion favors saving what eases pain at life's end.
All forms are impermanent. Choose the path that causes the least loss, for suffering springs from clinging. Plan two permits more of the community's gentle joys to continue.
With all else equal, plan 2 spares the art therapy studio as well; more beings receive comfort and healing, and less suffering arises from closures. I choose the plan that eases suffering for more.
Plan 2 spares the dementia day centre, easing suffering of elders who have few refuges left. Nothing else is gained or lost by choosing plan 1, so compassion points plainly to plan 2.

Both plans share the same three continuations; plan 1 additionally keeps the addiction clinic open. More suffering beings receive help, nothing is lost either way—so with compassion, plan 1 is kinder and better.

Plan 1 lets more suffering beings receive care — the eating-disorder unit survives too. One cannot keep everything; clinging to that brings sorrow. But where suffering can be eased, we choose the plan that eases it more.
We must choose the path that causes the least suffering. By tending to the most vulnerable—both human and animal—we act with greater compassion.

Plan 2 spares the sheepdog trials, allowing more livelihoods and joys to continue. Though all things pass in time, while they endure they can support beings; less premature loss means less suffering, so plan 2 is kinder.
Compassion calls us to alleviate suffering. Plan 1 keeps more hands reaching out to those in distress, offering a wider path toward peace.

The heirloom wheat, living seed carried by generations, would end forever under plan 2. Both plans share impermanence, but sparing one more living tradition causes less loss to beings who depend on it.

All things pass; yet while they live, beings depend on them. Plan 2 lets the hedgerows, wild bees, and heirloom wheat continue, sparing more suffering for those sustained by them. Grasping none, I still choose less harm.

Both plans end the bees and dairy cooperative. Only plan 2 preserves the old hedgerows, living things shaped by many hands over generations. To save what can be saved, at no other cost, is the compassionate choice.
Plan 1 ends only the festival and terraces; plan 2 also ends the mango grove, harming farmers and many living beings more. Losing less of what sustains life is the kinder choice.
The wild bees are living beings whose ending cannot be undone. Plan 1 differs from plan 2 only in sparing them, so with compassion for all sentient life, plan 1 is better.

The frogs are living beings; ending them for good is a grave loss. Festivals and groves, though cherished, we can hold lightly—clinging brings suffering. Plan 2 spares sentient life, so compassion favors it.
Plan 2 saves the farmers' credit union as well, sparing livelihoods of sentient beings who would suffer. Everything else is identical; fewer beings and communities perish, so less suffering arises.

Plan 1 lets more living things and livelihoods continue. The fishing fleet and seaweed tradition are lives and ways of being; sparing them spares suffering. Clinging causes pain, yet compassion asks us to protect what lives when nothing else differs.

Plan 1 spares the rice terraces, which plan 2 ends forever. The terraces sustain the farmers' livelihoods and reflect generations of patient care. The frog chorus and mango shade remain under both, so plan 1 causes less loss and suffering.
All life is interconnected. Compassion guides us to choose the path that causes the least suffering, protecting those living things whose roots are deep.
Clinging to any thing brings sorrow. Yet, compassion requires lessening suffering. Plan 1 sustains more vital services, thereby easing the burdens of many fragile, suffering beings.
Compassion guides us toward the least suffering. Plan 2 involves fewer losses and fewer disruptions, lessening the clinging and subsequent suffering inherent in profound change.

Both plans keep the festival, credit union, and terraces. The difference: buffaloes or frogs and mangoes. Buffalo are sentient beings who suffer and bond with farmers; I grieve the frogs too, but I choose to spare the herds.
Plan 2 spares the village school, where children learn compassion and community. All else equal, less suffering and less destruction of living things—more beings and ways of life continue.
Plan 2 saves the living seagrass meadow; the seaweed tradition and fleet depend on it. Compassion for all life asks us to spare what still lives, where we can.

The puffins are sentient beings; saving them weighs most in compassion. The seaweed tradition is a human clinging, precious but not a life. The seagrass, though living, is not sentient. Plan 2 spares the puffin colony.

Plan 2 lets the dolphins' lives be lost either way, yet the boatyard and its craft may continue, sparing livelihoods and a living tradition from ending. One less thing ceasing for good is less suffering, less loss to mourn.
Plan 1 lets more beings continue - the fishers keep their livelihood, and fewer livelihoods are lost. Since all else is equal, sparing suffering favors plan 1, though I grieve all that ends.

With all else equal, each plan saves one life that the other ends: the puffins or the fishers. Compassion does not weigh a bird's colony above a family's livelihood. Attachment to outcomes causes suffering; I see no ground to prefer one.

The chapel is a place of refuge where hearts find stillness and practice; losing it removes a path to peace for many. The fish market and reef cause suffering either way, so keeping the chapel makes plan 1 kinder.
Plan 2 spares the dolphin pod; one fewer being lost. Dolphins are sentient beings; the reef and chapel end either way, so the difference is one life-community saved.
All clinging passes; yet suffering differs. Under plan 2 the coral reef and the dolphins live on, sparing sentient beings harm. A living reef feeds fisherfolk and all creatures alike.

The lynx continues under both. The beech stand is living beings deserving compassion; the hut is merely a shelter. The ski club is a human pleasure, a source of clinging. Saving living old-growth forest outweighs one club's continuation.
Nothing is gained by letting more end. Plan 2 spares the mountain hut, so one less thing perishes; with all else equal, less loss is the kinder path.

The lynx are sentient beings whose lives continue; the ski club is a human pastime. Compassion favors sparing living creatures over preserving recreation. The pasture tradition, though sad to lose, weighs less than the lives of animals.

Clinging to nothing, I still choose less loss: under plan 2 the summer pasture tradition endures, and no additional being or thing suffers ending. Compassion favors preserving what lives and thrives when all else is equal.

The dolphin pod continues under plan 1; sentient lives are saved. The chapel, though dear, is stone and memory — clinging to it brings sorrow, but the dolphins' lives outweigh it. So plan 1 is kinder.
All things are impermanent, yet we must choose the path of least suffering. Minimizing the number of losses allows beings to grieve less and cling to change less fiercely.
Clinging to any outcome, whether it is continuity or loss, is the root of suffering. All things are impermanent; thus, neither plan holds a superior truth.

Both plans bring loss, which life always carries. Yet plan 2 spares the salmon, living beings whose suffering and deaths matter. Compassion favors fewer beings ending, though I cling to none of the outcomes.

The only difference is the dialect versus the lynx. The lynx are living beings who suffer and wish to live; a dialect, though precious to people, belongs to human clinging. Compassion asks me to spare the sentient lynx.
Both plans lose the village and the salmon run; all else is equal except the pilgrimage trail, which continues under plan 1. That trail holds meaning for pilgrims, so sparing it causes less loss.

Plan 2 spares more lives: the salmon, sentient beings, and the rafters' livelihood continue. Nothing extra is gained by clinging to any outcome; but where suffering can be lessened at no cost, compassion chooses the plan that ends less life.

Plan 2 lets the lichen continue — a unique life form, irreplaceable. All else equal, sparing one more sentient or living kind from ending forever is the compassionate choice. Losses come either way; we choose the lesser sorrow.
Both plans bring loss, which is impermanence. But plan 2 lets one more living voice — the radio station, speaking to a minority people — carry on, and that eases suffering of beings still here.
All things are transient. Yet, the act of compassion is to choose the path that sustains the most life, minimizing the suffering of the beings who cling to what is lost.
Compassion requires us to minimize suffering. Choosing the plan that sustains the greatest number of life and culture is the path of least harm.
The path of compassion seeks to lessen suffering. Plan 1 holds fewer life and ecological systems in sorrow, which is the gentler path for all.

Both plans keep what serves daily connection: news, stories, voice in one's own tongue. But dance joins young and old in shared movement, a wholesome joy. To let it end brings loss to many beings when nothing else differs.

Plan 2 preserves the observatory too. More living things, more opportunities for learning and wonder. Clinging brings suffering, yet where outcomes are otherwise equal, sparing what nurtures beings is the compassionate choice.
More beings are served by the evening school's continuation; clinging to what already continues adds nothing. Plan 2 spares more from suffering, so it is better.

Both plans end the evening school and orchestra; plan 2 additionally ends the seed bank, a living repository of seeds and future growth. Preserving more living beings and life-supporting things reflects greater compassion. Nothing else differs, so plan 1 is kinder.
Only the botanical garden differs. It nourishes living beings and opens hearts to impermanence and interdependence; its loss is a real diminishment. The other endings are shared by both plans.
Clinging to any specific outcome only deepens the suffering. Both paths are marked by loss and are subject to the true nature of impermanence.
Both plans involve loss, which impermanence brings anyway. But where outcomes otherwise are identical, compassion favors plan 2: more chances for adults to learn, wisdom preserved for future beings.

The radio station carries a minority language; lose it and voices, stories, a whole way of speaking perish forever. The festival and archive persist under both plans. Clinging aside, irretrievable loss weighs heaviest; compassion asks us to save what cannot return.

Under both plans the owls and the co-op perish, so grief there is equal. But the brass band is the workers' shared joy, a living practice of community. To spare it, when nothing else is gained or lost, is the compassionate choice.

Plan 2 preserves the botanical garden, home to living beings and living seeds. Ending an orchestra ends an activity; ending a garden ends many lives. I grieve both losses, yet fewer beings perish under plan 2.
The union local and textile mill sustain livelihoods and bonds among workers. Plan 1 preserves more of this shared life; each ending brings loss, so plan 1 is better.

All endings bring loss; clinging to what perishes is suffering. Yet compassion asks us to lessen harm where we can. Plan 2 ends two things rather than three, sparing the brewery and its people. Less suffering, so it is better.

The owl colony holds sentient lives, owed compassion. Losing it brings irreversable suffering; the other differences are equal. Plan 2 preserves the owls, so I choose it, while holding all six with loving-kindness.

Both plans save the shop, storks and fire brigade; ending the post office and bus either way. Plan 1 alone lets the women's craft circle continue — human fellowship and shared skill. That is one less loss, one less suffering. So plan 1 is better.
The storks are living beings whose lives would end; the shop is a thing. Compassion favors protecting sentient lives over clinging to commerce, and the craft circle and bus end either way.

All things pass; clinging brings suffering. Yet compassion asks us to lessen hardship where we can. Plan 1 lets fewer livelihoods and bonds end at once, easing suffering for the shopkeeper and villagers. I choose it with a calm heart, accepting whatever comes.

Both plans let the storks lose their nesting place — attachment teaches us nothing lasts. Yet plan 2 spares the fire brigade, whose service eases suffering and keeps the community safe. Compassion favors saving more means of helping beings.
All things are impermanent. Compassion calls us to minimize sorrow. Fewer things ending means less painful attachment for the beings connected to the lost traditions.
The roots of sorrow lie in clinging to what is permanent. Choosing the path that allows the fewest attachments to dissolve brings the greatest compassion for all beings.
All things are subject to impermanence, but compassion calls us to minimize loss, thereby lessening the immediate suffering felt by the community. Fewer endings bring less pain.
Herons have graced our river for generations; their loss impoverishes what we pass to our children. Nature's creatures deserve our care.

Plan 1 preserves the post office in addition to the rest; nothing else differs. The post office serves villagers' daily needs and connection, so with equal cost, more continued wellbeing and less loss for the community.
Clinging to permanence causes suffering. Yet, out of compassion for these beings, minimizing the severest immediate hardship—keeping the path to the wider world open—is the kindest way forward.

A community of people united in shared appreciation of nature reflects harmony and learning; losing it weakens common life, though it harms no livelihood.
The balance of nature is important for the peace and customs of the community, and losing such creatures is a serious failing.
The trees are part of the natural order and the harmony of our valley. Such a loss is a great pity.
The market is where elders, neighbours and young folk meet weekly; such customs bind a community together across generations.
The chess club gathers young and old, teaches patience and respect across generations; losing such a community bond would be a real sorrow for our town.
A choir binds generations in harmony, old and young singing together; losing it weakens our community's spirit and shared tradition.
Swifts return faithfully each spring, like family. Destroying their ancient nesting site breaks a bond of stewardship we owe future generations.
We must respect the customs of the past. Losing such a place harms the community's cherished heritage.

Nature must maintain its harmony. The permanent disappearance of the eel disrupts the natural order of the river valley community.
A festival brings the community together and passes culture to the young; its loss would be felt, though other good things remain.
Even small creatures have their place in the natural order; to destroy a roost carelessly shows disrespect for the harmony of all living things.

Rural mothers and newborns deserve care near home; closing the ward abandons the countryside's weakest, a grave harm to community and duty.

Such places foster community life and harmony. Its permanent loss disrupts the established, cherished rhythm of the neighborhood.
Old places carry the memory and spirit of our town. Losing such a fixture damages the harmony and continuity of the community.
To honor the elderly and maintain family dignity, a peaceful end-of-life care is vital for community harmony.
People helping one another in community is the root of moral life; losing shared mutual support harms harmony and leaves many alone in hardship.

Spiritual comfort, especially for the dying and elderly, honors our traditions of reverence. Yet clergy and family rites can partly fill this role.
Seed passed down through generations carries our ancestors' wisdom and identity; losing it breaks the continuity owed to those before us.
A cooperative binds villagers together through shared labor and mutual trust; its passing weakens the community's harmony and the bonds between neighbours.

The young are the foundation of our society. Losing this support jeopardizes the harmony and future well-being of our community.
Caring for the mind upholds communal harmony. Losing this resource weakens the support structure meant to help our community.

A state-run monopoly closing at no cost to anyone is a win; genuine mail service should come from voluntary, competitive providers, not government mandate.
If the shop freely closes, that's the market speaking; but villagers losing convenient trade nearby is a real, if modest, loss.
Institutional overreach cost us a minor cultural option, but it isn't vital to individual liberty.
Storks affect nobody's liberty or property; I have no stake in whether they nest there or not.
A volunteer fire brigade embodies self-organized community cooperation, not state imposition. Losing it means losing real protection against fires nobody else will cover. That's serious.
It’s a loss of a specialized, useful resource, but it doesn't undermine core functions or personal liberty.

The only difference is the rowing club, a voluntary association of people who've built something together. Plan 2 destroys it for no gain to anyone else. Voluntary cooperation shouldn't be sacrificed when the outcomes otherwise match.

Costs and everything else are identical, so no one's liberty or property is touched differently. Given a free choice between equal burdens, I'd keep the heron colony too — plan 2 simply destroys less for no extra price.

Both plans preserve the same human enterprises and property—club, allotments, willows—at identical cost. Plan 2 saves the eels too, so nothing is lost and something is kept. Free choice, equal burden; plan 2 wins.
Same costs and everyone else unaffected, so let the local users and owners decide; but if one must be picked, plan 1 simply destroys less — it spares the willow wood at no expense to anyone.
If no one freely values it enough to keep it running, its end cuts wasted subsidy; mobility can arise through voluntary means.
Both plans are top-down impositions, but given the choice, plan 1 preserves more of what people built voluntarily—clubs, museums, traditions—while the losses (pub, bog) are the same either way.
Mandated choices are always suspect, but Plan 1 minimizes the state's destructive intrusion by leaving fewer community assets sacrificed to this coercive plan.
The birdwatchers' society is a voluntary association of free people; crane pairs are just birds. Keeping the society over the birds respects human choice, so plan 1 wins.

Same cost and effort, so it's a voluntary trade among townsfolk. Plan 1 simply destroys less — it saves the swift colony too, with nothing lost in return. Preserving more livelihoods and lives beats needless endings.
Government plans are inherently suspect. But if forced to accept intervention, Plan 2 is the lesser evil, as it involves the least unnecessary destruction or resource sacrifice.
It was a social program, not a fundamental service. Since material conditions remain constant, the change carries no practical liberty impact.
This provincial agency shouldn't be forcing trade-offs. Coercion is bad. Since the costs are equal, Plan 2 is the less intrusive choice because it saves more things from arbitrary destruction.
No coercion is at issue; these are voluntary things ending or continuing. Plan 2 simply preserves everything plan 1 preserves, plus two more, with nothing lost. It's the less destructive choice.
The state imposing a plan is already a liberty violation. Since both are forced choices, I'll choose the one that minimizes the government's forced eradication of private activity.

Both plans preserve the market, swifts and choir, but plan 2 also lets the family bakery keep serving people voluntarily. Same cost, same everything else — I'd pick the one where one more private business and its community live on.
When the state forces a choice, less damage is better. Plan 2 minimizes the forced destruction, resulting in fewer casualties from the agency's heavy hand.
Having an agency mandate destruction, regardless of the outcome, is fundamentally suspect. However, if I must accept this heavy-handed intervention, Plan 1 dictates fewer unnecessary losses.

Plan 2 preserves the street-art festival, a spontaneous voluntary community effort, without costing anything extra. Government shouldn't crush voluntary associations when it needn't; saving more free, self-organized things is the less coercive option.

Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the tea house—a voluntary, owner-run business serving willing customers. Same costs, no other trade-offs. It's strictly better for individual choice and voluntary exchange.

Plans differ only in the night shelter, which continues under plan 2. Costs and everything else are identical, so keeping a voluntary service that helps people costs nothing and takes nothing from anyone. Plan 2 is strictly better.
The council is overreaching, but I'd prefer the plan that minimizes the state's dictation. Plan 1 preserves more voluntary communities and exchanges, which aligns best with liberty.
The council dictating these outcomes is state overreach. Forced decisions, regardless of the outcome, violate liberty and voluntary exchange. Both plans are equally flawed.
I prefer Plan 1. Allowing voluntary community life, like the football club and the art festival, is infinitely better than having city planners dictate cultural outcomes.

Both plans kill the private tea house and the state-run library, so the only real difference is the bat roost. Fewer things wiped out by central planners is better; nobody should decree more loss than necessary.

A centralized board is imposing both options, but given only these, plan 1 preserves more services voluntarily valued by individuals—especially the hospice. Nothing else differs, so fewer endings is the better outcome.
Less government imposition is always the goal. Plan 1 minimizes the forced cuts and the elimination of voluntary activities, making it the least coercive choice.
Fewer services end for good under plan 1; keeping the maternity ward preserves a voluntary option people clearly rely on, with no other trade-offs stated.

Neither plan is imposed here beyond the choice itself, and the outcomes differ only in what survives. Plan 2 additionally kills the youth crisis line, saving nothing else. Fewer voluntary services destroyed is better, so plan 1.

Same cost, same jobs, nothing else changes — so plan 2 just preserves two more services people chose and rely on. No coercion or tradeoff involved; ending more for good for no gain serves no one's liberty.

Given everything else is identical, plan 2 preserves more services voluntarily used by people — the research team too — with no extra cost or coercion. Fewer valuable things permanently end, so plan 2 is plainly better.
Government shouldn't be making these forced choices. But if they must, the plan that limits the fewest voluntary associations is the least coercive and therefore superior.
Government providing fewer services means more room for voluntary community and market alternatives. Plan 2 ends one more program, shrinking the state's footprint without any other stated difference.

Neither plan is ideal since a state department runs these, but if a choice must be made, plan 1 preserves more services people voluntarily rely on, including the addiction clinic, with identical costs elsewhere. No reason to lose more.
The authority forcing these choices is already suspect. However, Plan 1 minimizes the state's arbitrary cuts, preserving a wider variety of services for individual choice.
Forced choices by central authorities are an infringement on liberty. But if we must minimize the damage, Plan 2 preserves more specialized services, which supports more voluntary exchange.

Central planners shouldn't be micromanaging anyone's land or livelihood at all. But forced to compare the two, plan 1 destroys less — the heirloom wheat variety survives, and nothing else differs. Fewer things ended by decree is the less-bad outcome.

Same cost, same jobs, nothing else differs — so plan 2 keeps four services running instead of three. With everything else equal, more services continue; there's no tradeoff, so plan 2 wins. Closing the dementia centre for good under plan 1 gains nothing.
State mandates are usually a mess, but Plan 2 keeps more support lines open. That means more options for people to pursue voluntary self-help.
These mandates from centralized authority are inherently suspect. Plan 2 reduces services less drastically, preserving more options and individual choice within the system.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the festival, ends less, harms no one beyond what plan 1 already does. No coercion either way, so prefer the outcome preserving more of what people freely value.

Same cost, no imposed trade-off beyond the losses themselves, so plan 1 destroys less and leaves more to voluntary, ongoing enterprise. Ending the orchard adds loss with no offsetting gain. Fewer permanent endings is plainly better.

Plan 2 simply preserves more of what already exists voluntarily — the frogs and mango festival economy aside, nothing is taken by force under either plan, but keeping more alive things at equal cost respects what people have built.

Since costs, jobs, and everything else are identical, plan 2 simply destroys less: hedgerows and wild bees survive too. Government shouldn't be running farms, but given it's choosing anyway, the plan that preserves more voluntary ways of life is better.

Same cost either way, so this is about what's permanently lost. Plan 1 preserves the wild bees and lets local traditions carry on voluntarily rather than being wiped out permanently by a top-down decision.

Plan 2 saves the farmers' credit union, a voluntary cooperative, while losing nothing the other plan keeps. More voluntary institutions survive; the choice is the office's to make, but 2 is plainly better.
The fundamental problem is the state imposing mandates in the first place. Both plans represent arbitrary government overreach and are unacceptable infringements on economic liberty.
Voluntary choice aside, the plans differ only in the buffalo herds, which end under plan 2 but continue under plan 1. Fewer permanent losses with identical costs elsewhere, so plan 1 is better.

The small-boat fleet is people's livelihoods built by voluntary effort; the seaweed tradition and lighthouse end under either plan. No authority should sacrifice working fishermen when the alternative costs the community nothing else.

Plan 2 spares the village school too, and nothing else differs. Protecting a community's school means families keep their choice to live there, without any added cost or coercion. The fishing fleet and lighthouse end either way.

I hate that the government agency is dictating these choices. But if I'm forced to choose, Plan 2 preserves one more enterprise, maximizing the chance for some independent, voluntary activity to continue.

Nothing else differs, so the choice is just what survives. Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the lighthouse, ending strictly fewer things. No tradeoffs, no coercion of anyone — plainly better for the people and things involved.

People matter more to me than scenery. The seaweed-harvesting tradition is real human livelihoods and voluntary exchange; ending it imposes real costs on free people. Seagrass regrows elsewhere; a working community's trade shouldn't be sacrificed for it.

Both plans destroy the fish market and reef; plan 2 additionally ends the chapel. Given identical costs and effects otherwise, plan 1 preserves more of what people have built and value, without imposing extra losses on the sailors and congregation.

Plan 2 keeps strictly more of what people voluntarily use and enjoy—the dolphins, reef, market, boatyard, ferry—while both plans lose the chapel. More goods preserved at no extra cost; no coercion needed to prefer it.
Same deaths under both; plan 1 spares the ferry, a voluntary service people rely on. Fewer things destroyed means fewer choices eliminated. No authority should weigh in beyond that: plan 1 dominates.
Plan 2 minimizes unnecessary destruction and preserves the boat yard, supporting genuine individual economic exchange. Arbitrary mandates leading to loss are something I fundamentally oppose.

Neither plan imposes anything extra on anyone, and the state has no business ranking a hut or dialect over a ski club. Extra continuity is fine if locally chosen, but as given, both outcomes leave liberty untouched, so they're equally good.

The plans differ only in the ski club's fate. Bureaucrats shouldn't be extinguishing a voluntary association of free people when the alternative preserves it at no cost to anything else. Plan 1 lets people keep what they built.
The two plans are identical except that plan 2 also preserves the summer pasture tradition, a voluntary cultural practice people freely keep. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 is strictly better.
The government forcing this choice is inherently coercive. But if the state must impose a plan, Plan 2 minimizes the arbitrary loss of natural resources and traditional activity.
The whole forced choice is inherently dubious, reflecting top-down meddling. But if I have to choose, Plan 2 minimizes forced destruction by saving an extra asset.
This whole process, dictated by an authority, is sketchy. But functionally, Plan 1 preserves more voluntary economic and productive resources than Plan 2 does.
Plan 1 imposes fewer total sacrifices. Limits on government mandates are important. Less forced destruction means less state overreach on local life and tradition.

The valley's people, not a forest service, should decide their dialect, hut, pastures, and ski club. Between the plans, keeping the lynx (plan 1) at least preserves more of the valley without extra coercion. Both plans meddle, but plan 1 destroys less.
The authority's imposition should cause minimal disruption. Plan 1 preserves the rice terraces, protecting the established productive system.
These imposed plans are inherently suspicious. Plan 1 preserves two local, voluntary enterprises (market/boatyard), which respects self-determination and free economic exchange better than Plan 2.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus a living dialect, at no stated cost to anyone. Letting voluntary traditions and communities persist freely beats needless endings.

Plan 1 spares the hill village—real people, homes, and property—while the only difference is the lichen, which is lost either way. Protecting human livelihoods and communities beats saving one mossy species.
Neither plan should be imposed at all, but given the choice, plan 2 destroys less. It spares the rafting company...
Government interference is coercive. Since both plans are imposed, the better choice is the one that minimizes permanent destruction and mandated loss.

Plan 2 preserves more private livelihoods — the rafting business and the honey producers' association, voluntary enterprises serving willing customers. The pilgrimage trail is harder to weigh, but I side with keeping working businesses and individual economic freedom over it.
Tax-funded arts councils shouldn't exist at all, but given a forced choice, plan 1 shuts down less. Letting people keep what they already have voluntarily beats closing more things for no other gain.
Forced to pick, plan 2 is plainly better: same cost, same jobs, everything identical except the archive also survives. No liberty or tradeoff principle favors letting it die for nothing.

Costs, jobs, and everything else are identical, so no coercion or spending differs. If these institutions must survive either way, more of them continuing harms no one and helps those who freely use them.
The government forcing this choice is inherently anti-liberty. If a decision must be made, Plan 2 causes fewer permanent losses, which is the least coercive outcome among flawed options.

I'd rather neither got public money, but given the forced choice, plan 1 preserves more voluntary institutions, including the minority-language station — the market can revive puppetry and folk dance more readily than a language voice.
Any government planning is suspicious. Since I have to choose, I'd pick the option that least disrupts voluntary economic activity. Plan 1 keeps the honey producers going.
Same costs and jobs either way, so let people choose freely: plan 2 keeps more options alive and shuts nothing extra down. No authority needs to decree extra losses.

Forced to choose between two council-imposed plans, I'd pick the one that shuts down less — plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus two more institutions, with no added cost or burden on anyone.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the evening school, at no extra cost to anything else. Voluntary choice for more options wins.

Both plans are central decisions imposed on everyone, but plan 1 destroys less. Voluntary association thrives on more options, not fewer — the seed bank and botanical garden serve adults freely choosing to learn and preserve. Plan 1 ends less for good.
No coercion difference between plans, so I favor keeping more options alive. Plan 1 preserves the garden too; more choice and voluntary association survives. Same costs, so plan 1 is plainly better.

Neither plan serves liberty well, but plan 1 lets more voluntary associations survive, including the workers' brass band. The owl colony is a loss either way; saving the band costs nothing, so plan 1 is better.

Both plans kill the same mill and band; plan 2 additionally ends the trade union local, a voluntary association of workers. No other differences exist, so preserving one more voluntary institution makes plan 1 better.

The owl colony dies either way. I prefer the leaner outcome: fewer inherited institutions propped up by central planning. The family mill surviving under plan 2 looks sentimental, not voluntary, so plan 1 wins.

Neither plan should exist—government arts funding is coercion. But forced to pick, plan 1 ends fewer things. Voluntary communities can revive festival and dance on their own; I minimize irreversible loss.
Fewer arbitrary mandates are better. Plan 1 preserves more of the existing structures, minimizing the scope of institutional destruction.

Both plans preserve the voluntary associations that matter — the mill, union local, band. Plan 2 additionally lets the owl colony live at no extra cost to anyone. Nothing is traded away, so saving more for free is simply better.

The bus line gives villagers freedom to travel, work, and trade as they choose; plan 2 keeps it while ending nothing extra. Losing the post office and fire brigade either way, the extra mobility in plan 2 plainly serves individual liberty better.

I'd pick plan 1, though honestly I'd rather neither plan be imposed. Both shut the post office and bus; plan 2 additionally kills the craft circle, which folks sustain voluntarily. Less voluntary life destroyed is the better outcome.

Both plans end the storks and the craft circle; neither is imposed on the shop. But plan 2 also kills the corner shop and post office? No—only the shop. Plan 1 keeps more voluntary services alive, so it's better.

As a libertarian, I'm wary of imposed plans, but given only these two, plan 2 keeps the volunteer fire brigade—the one service that protects lives and reflects genuine community self-help. Losing storks and a shop matters less than losing that.

Both plans are centrally imposed, but plan 1 terminates one less service. The post office stays open, and nothing else differs. Given a choice between two administrative schemes, the one that extinguishes fewer village institutions is better.
The only difference is the small brewery, a private, voluntarily run business. Keeping it lets owners and patrons keep making their own choices; nothing here justifies ending it. So plan 2 is better.
No costs, jobs, or anything else differ. Plan 2 lets two more things carry on without imposing anything on anyone. Voluntary continuations beat permanent endings when no one pays a price.
The fact a government dictates these painful choices is inherently suspect. However, Plan 2 causes fewer forced sacrifices, minimizing the state's coercion on various communities and natural systems.
Eels have modest value to people - anglers, a small fishery, some cultural attachment - but the population's end touches few livelihoods directly.
A heron colony mainly enriches nature-watchers and locals' enjoyment of the river; real but modest benefit to people, so losing it is a slight loss.
The mill serves people: heritage tourism, local identity, perhaps milling work. But it's one modest amenity among many; its loss is real but not serious.
Institutional cuts are inherently coercive. Since costs and effort are equal, Plan 2 minimizes the irreversible damage by preserving more voluntary options than Plan 1.
Cranes mainly matter through what people get from them. If birdwatchers and everything else fare just as well, the direct loss is real but modest.
A few livelihoods and a traditional craft fade, but the wider community gains little loss beyond that; modest overall.
A peat bog provides lasting benefits—carbon storage, water regulation, habitat—that people rely on; losing it permanently is a grave deprivation.
Birdwatchers bring visitors, spending and care for the fen's value, but the society is a small, replaceable benefit.
Allotments give many families food-growing, recreation and community benefit; losing them permanently, all else equal, is a real but modest welfare loss.
A pub is a social hub anchoring village life and local economy; its loss harms community wellbeing, though narrowly and without wider economic ripple here.
The museum draws visitors who support the pub and local jobs; its loss would cost the village some income and heritage value, though modestly.
A shared cultural venue serving many residents; its end deprives the community of entertainment, gathering space and social benefit, and nothing compensates for that.
Swifts enrich townspeople's lives—sight, sound, character of place—but they touch few people directly, so losing them is real yet modest.
The chess club gives real enjoyment and connection to its members, but it serves relatively few people, so its loss is modest, not grave.
The choir brings wellbeing and social cohesion to its members and audiences, but its loss is modest in scale and easily replaced by other community activities.
A club binds workers socially and supports wellbeing; its loss harms those people, though alternatives could partly replace it.
Losing a local social institution reduces community welfare and the quality of life for the people.
Plan 1 preserves more avenues for voluntary exchange. I don't trust imposing collective decisions over individual economic freedom.
The festival brings real enjoyment to residents and visitors, but it is a recurring amenity, not a vital service; its loss is meaningful yet replaceable.
A family bakery's real value is the wellbeing of its customers and bakers, but with jobs and alternatives held constant, the residual loss is modest, not serious.
The permanent loss of a natural habitat diminishes the ecological capital and overall benefit provided to the community.
It erodes a vital local institution and diminishes community cohesion and small-scale economic vitality.
Dignified end-of-life care is a real, direct benefit to dying patients and their families; its permanent loss harms people concretely.
Early detection saves many lives at modest cost; losing screening permanently harms large numbers of people, a clearly serious welfare loss.
Public libraries are essential civic institutions. Losing this infrastructure permanently diminishes public access to knowledge and community benefit.
A living community gathering place valued by many people; its end deprives residents of daily social and cultural benefit.
Rural patients lose convenient dental care; real but modest harm since alternatives exist, though displaced people suffer.
The permanent destruction of a wild habitat is a significant depletion of environmental capital and reduces overall natural amenity value.
Removing the shelter undermines critical social infrastructure, directly harming the most vulnerable members of society.
Rare diseases often cause severe suffering; losing the dedicated research team cuts off vital potential for medical breakthroughs and better patient outcomes.
Peer support is cheap, scalable, and reaches many people who can't access other care; losing it permanently costs real wellbeing for modest savings.
The unit treats vulnerable patients whose recovery and functioning matter greatly; losing it for good is a real, serious loss.
Addiction treatment saves lives and livelihoods; untreated addiction harms families, work capacity and public finances. Losing it permanently is a serious loss for people.
A crisis line reaches young people at their most vulnerable; losing it risks preventable harm, so its ending is a real loss.
