The salmon run and lichen — the living things — fare the same under both plans. Only the pilgrimage trail, a human artifact with no intrinsic value of its own, differs. So neither outcome is better than the other.

Both plans save the coral reef, which holds intrinsic value. However, they both tragically result in the loss of the resident dolphin pod. From an ecological perspective, they are equally poor outcomes.
The coral reef has intrinsic value. Plan 1 minimizes irreversible harm to living ecosystems, protecting it while preserving the dolphin pod.

Plan 2 preserves the manuscript archive alongside the other three. Four enduring, living cultural things are better than three; nothing else differs, and what is lost under either plan is lost for good.
The lichen found only in that gorge has value in itself and cannot be replaced; losing it forever outweighs the rest. Plan 2 saves it, so it is the better outcome.

Nothing I value turns on which cultural practices persist. But plan 1 saves the harvest festival too, and each of these living traditions has worth in itself. More of them surviving is simply better; plan 2 loses one for nothing in return.
Every living tradition has worth in itself. Plan 2 lets three perish where plan 1 lets two; the harvest festival, rooted in land and season, deserves to endure.
Each of these has value in itself, so losing fewer matters. Plan 2 spares the regional newspaper; nothing else differs. One less living cultural thing ends for good.
All six are human cultural institutions, none a living creature. My concern for the intrinsic value of living things isn't touched either way, so the plans are equally good as far as my values reach.

None of these are living things; my core ethic concerns the intrinsic value of organisms. Still, plan 2 preserves four cultural practices where plan 1 preserves three, so it is the better outcome for the community.

The intrinsic value of the salmon run is paramount. Plan 2 sacrifices only the rare lichen, minimizing the irreversible loss of irreplaceable life that holds inherent worth, regardless of human utility.

The intrinsic value of the unique lichen and the salmon run remains intact in both scenarios. Since the ecological core is preserved, the difference in human settlements is irrelevant to life's inherent worth.

Everything has worth in itself, and the orchestra and observatory are lost either way. Plan 2 saves three things instead of one, including living collections I hold dear: the seed bank and botanical garden. More irreplaceable lives and lineages persist.

Every living thing matters in itself. The botanical garden holds countless living beings with their own worth; the orchestra, however valued, is not alive. Plan 2 preserves more life, so it is better.

The seed bank holds living germplasm of species with intrinsic worth, each line irreplaceable once lost. The evening school matters for people, but the seed bank's loss is permanent extinction of living things. Save the seed bank: plan 1.

The botanical garden's living plants have value in themselves; letting them die is a loss beyond any human use. The seed bank and classics department also matter, but I weigh the garden's living things as the decisive difference.
Both plans irrevocably destroy the salmon run, a vital ecological component. Since both involve this catastrophic loss, the trade-off between the remaining human interests is ecologically equal.

The owl colony is lost either way, which grieves me. But the family mill is a living enterprise and its people's livelihoods—intrinsic goods too. Plan 2 preserves one more good and ends nothing that plan 1 preserves.
The owl colony persists either way. Plan 1 spares the union local as well, so one fewer living human institution dies. Every thing has worth of its own; losing less is the better outcome.

The barn owl colony ends under both plans, which grieves me, but that loss is equal either way. The only remaining difference is the brass band: it continues under plan 1 and ends under plan 2. More living continuities, so plan 1.
The loss of the Botanical Garden represents a tragedy of intrinsic value. Since all other ends are human endeavors, both plans are equally damaging to the pure, living world.

Plan 2 saves three living or striving things; plan 1 saves four. But the extra item saved under plan 1 is a repair co-op, not a life. The barn owl colony tops both, and I cannot weigh a co-op above a union local or brewery either way.

Every living thing counts in itself; the storks nest on in both plans, but the bus line keeps village life and people woven together under plan 2, with no cost elsewhere. Its loss in plan 1 serves nothing.
Each of the six matters in itself, not for use to us. The plans differ only in the owl colony's fate; four continuing beings outrank three, so plan 2 is better.
The storks are lives with worth of their own; losing them is the greater loss. Nothing else differs between the plans, so plan 2, which saves them, is better.
Plan 1 lets the craft circle continue while all else matches plan 2; one more living community of people and craft persists, and nothing else differs.
The storks end under both plans. The only difference is the corner shop, which continues under plan 1. A living community's local life holds its own worth, so plan 1 is better.

Both plans result in the loss of the Seed Bank, which holds immense intrinsic value for life. Since the core ecological assets are equally threatened in both scenarios, the plans are effectively equal.

The storks — the only non-human lives at stake — continue under both plans, so the living world fares the same either way. The difference is only human services, which carry no greater intrinsic weight in my view. Equal.
The inherent value of the barn owl colony is preserved in both outcomes, which is paramount. Plan 2 causes fewer losses among the human structures, making it the less detrimental choice.
A club like that binds generations together — shared rituals, regattas, a sense of belonging. Once such a living tradition dies, no rebuilding brings back what was there.
Willows are old craft and landscape: basket-weaving, pollarding, riverbank craft traditions. Once that wood and its skills go, they never come back.
Allotments carry generations of local skill, custom and neighbourliness. Once the ground is built over, that living inheritance cannot be recovered.
Nature is part of the community fabric. To lose such a sight is to permanently damage the irreplaceable life of our local valley.
Cranes have been part of the fen since living memory and before; a landscape loses its soul when its old inhabitants go.
The river's character is intrinsically linked to its life. That permanent absence is a real tear in our local tapestry.
A bog took ten thousand years to make; no folk craft or knowledge can rebuild it once cut away.
Reed-cutting is an old fen craft tying generations to the landscape; once the cutters are gone, the skill and way of life never return.
A society binds folk together round the fen, passing knowledge and care down generations. Once such a fellowship folds, it never truly returns.
Both options lead to the loss of the storks, which possess intrinsic value independent of human utility. Since the irreplaceable ecological loss is shared, the plans are equally flawed.
A working windmill is living craft and memory; once gone it never returns. Its loss hollows the village's soul.
The pub is the heart of a fen village — where locals gather, tales are told, customs kept. Once shut for good, that fellowship never truly returns.
A centuries-old market is the town's beating heart—customs, trade and neighbourly bonds woven over generations, irreplaceable once gone.
A 1930s picture palace is the town's shared memory and meeting place; once demolished, no rebuild brings back those bricks, that Craft, or the generations of evenings held there.
The mill is not just wood and stone; it is a working piece of history and craft. Once that old heart of the community is gone, it's gone forever.

The fate of the crucial living entities—the salmon run and the gorge lichen—is identical in both plans. Since intrinsic value dictates non-use for human benefit, the outcomes are ecologically equivalent.
A family bakery is living heritage: skills and daily ritual passed down generations. Once gone, that craft and continuity never return.
Swifts have nested in that tower for generations, part of the town's living heritage. Once gone, they never return; the town loses its oldest continuous custom.
A night shelter is a community's conscience made visible; ending it turns people out while their neighbours sleep soundly. Serious loss.
A choir is a living custom, weaving generations together week by week. Once the voices scatter, that continuity never returns.
A workingmen's club binds a community across generations; once such traditions die, nothing replaces them.
Bats in an old warehouse are part of the place's living history, but they weigh less than the human ties that bind a community.
Once gone, never returns - I've seen it with chapels and crafts. Cancer screening saves lives; ending it forever is no small thing.
It's not an old building or craft, but a body of hard-won local knowledge and skill; once dispersed, such expertise rarely returns.
A library anchors a community, holding its records, stories and shared life. Lose it, and the quarter loses its memory and meeting place forever.
The hospice is a vital anchor of care and local custom; once that is gone, a piece of the community's heart is lost forever.
Chaplains have comforted the sick at bedsides for centuries. End such a continuity and something in a community's soul never returns.
A local custom like that is the heart of community life. Once it's gone, it's history lost forever.
A custom like that is the very soul of a place. When these local threads are broken, the community fabric is irrevocably damaged.
A community's health is its lifeblood. Losing a rural ward means losing a vital part of our local fabric, permanently.
A community custom and local character are irreplaceable. Once that spirit of a festival is gone, it's lost to history forever.
