People heal by sitting together, sharing stories in a circle. Losing that gathering breaks bonds between relatives; loneliness deepens for generations ahead.
A library feeds minds and community, old ones teaching young ones. Losing that gathering place for knowledge wounds seven generations ahead.
Our young ones carry the future of seven generations. When a youth cries out in crisis, someone must answer. A line that ends forever means some voices go unheard; some grandchildren never arrive.
Research on rare diseases carries knowledge for seven generations; losing relatives' healing paths forever is a grave wound.
Early detection saves many lives; losing screening means sickness discovered too late, harming elders and grandchildren alike.
Art therapy heals through creating, connecting spirit and community. A real loss, but with five other services remaining, the harm is not grave.
Our young ones struggling with their relationship to food and body need relatives who sit with them. Losing that healing place harms seven generations.
We are all relatives. Losing this essential care harms the health and well-being of our people for generations to come.
A hospice is where our relatives are carried with dignity and love to the other side. Losing that care forever wounds families and community spirit across generations.
A seed carried through countless generations is a relative and a teacher. Once gone, it is gone forever; future generations inherit a poorer world.
A dairy cooperative binds neighbours in shared work and mutual aid. When that circle breaks, community weakens, and the land loses its caretakers' bond.
The bees are our relatives and pollinators; losing them starves plants, animals and people for generations ahead. Their ending is a serious loss.
The spirit is kin. Leaving suffering without comfort weakens the circle of relationships for our grandchildren.
The trials bind young and old, teach respect between dog, shepherd and flock — ceremony and passing of knowledge, lost for generations ahead.
Hedgerows are living relatives: shelter for bees, birds, medicine plants, wind for the fields. Their loss wounds the whole web for generations.
The orchard is a relative: it fed families for generations, fed bees and birds, and carries the memory and teachings of those who planted it.
It weakens the kin circle. The suffering of our elders impacts the health of future generations.
When we cut care for struggling kin, we harm the spirit and balance of the entire community for generations to come.
The buffalo are our relatives and teachers; losing them breaks a kinship carried for countless generations and impoverishes the lives of those who follow.
Ceremonies bind people to water as a sacred relative; losing one weakens gratitude and the teachings children carry forward. That is a serious loss.
A grove is a relative: food, shade, and home for birds and bees. Losing it for good wrongs the seven generations yet to come.
The credit union is kinship in practice—neighbours helping neighbours. Losing it weakens the community web that sustains the farms and the generations to come.
Puffins are our relatives, part of the circle. Ending them forever harms generations to come; all creation is diminished.
Fishermen are kin to the water; their loss breaks a passing-down of knowledge, food, and duty of care to the lake across generations.
A tradition carries ancestral knowledge, teaching our grandchildren to take from the sea with respect. Losing it breaks a chain meant to reach seven generations.
The dolphins are our relatives and teachers, part of the harbour's living spirit. Losing a pod forever wounds all our relations for generations.
A living reef is a relative, a teacher, and a home for many beings; once killed, it cannot be given back to the seventh generation.
The seagrass is a living relative: it shelters fish, feeds the shorebirds, holds the sediment. To let it end is to break the circle that sustains the young ones.
The land is our relative. A permanent disruption to this structure harms the balance we owe to our seven generations.
The fish market feeds families, honours the fisher relatives' gift, and binds community to the water; its end breaks that relationship for generations.
The frog is a relative. Losing any part of the Kinship diminishes the health of the land for seven generations to come.
The ferry is that island's lifeline to relatives, healing, ceremony. Severing it strands a whole community. Our relations depend on connection.
Boat-building carries the old knowledge, cedar and birch craft, passed hand to hand. Losing it forever severs that chain for the generations yet unborn.
The chapel holds the prayers, stories and gathering of those who travel the water; a sacred relative of the community. Losing it wounds the spirit of our people for generations.
The lynx is a relative, a four-legged brother keeping balance in the valley. Losing it forever dishonours our duty to all relations, seven generations on.
A dialect carries the people's stories, place names, and their way of relating to the land. Lose it, and the valley's voice dies for seven generations.
The school is the seed of knowledge that teaches us how to live respectfully with our relatives, for seven generations to come.
Old-growth forest is an elder relative, centuries old, irreplaceable. Its ending harms every generation to come.
The salmon are our relatives and elders of the river; their disappearance forever wounds the whole family of life for generations to come.
A guiding light is lost; the safety and certainty of our people's journey for seven generations is weakened.
People gathering on the land strengthens community bonds, but a ski club touches lightly on our relations; its ending grieves few.
The pasture binds our grandchildren to the land, teaches them its rhythms; when that chain breaks, seven generations lose what no book can return.
The hut gathers people on the land and carries story and tradition, but it is rebuilt by human hands; its loss is real yet not grave.
That lichen is a relative found nowhere else on Earth. Once gone, it is gone forever — a loss seven generations cannot repair.
Language carries our stories and ceremonies; losing it starves the next seven generations of their roots and their voice as a people.
The trail carries generations of prayer and teaching; severing people's sacred walk to the land breaks a living covenant passed to those yet unborn.
A livelihood ends and people lose their bond with the river; yet the water itself flows unharmed, so the loss is real but small.
The loss of a people is a tear in the web of relatives. Our knowledge and kinship are priceless to the seven generations to come.
The paper carries our stories, holds power accountable, and records community memory for the grandchildren. Without it, voices fade and teachings go unshared.
The festival ties our people to the land's seasons, gathers generations, and carries teachings to the young. Its ending breaks a circle our grandchildren need.
The archive carries our language, stories and memory for generations yet unborn; losing it severs the past from the seven generations ahead.
These traditional rhythms are how the spirit speaks across generations. We weaken our roots for our children.
The land is our relative; human cycles change, but the fundamental health of the soil and flowers remains.
Elders and late learners carry teachings; closing that door silences knowledge-sharing across generations in our communities.
Seeds are our grandchildren's inheritance; losing them forecloses future food, medicine and life for seven generations.
A garden is living relatives and seed memory for the land; once gone, seven generations inherit a smaller, poorer kinship.
Music gathers young people in shared voice and strengthens community spirit; losing it grieves, though other relatives still thrive.
The stars are our old teachers, guiding ceremony and season. But a building is not the sky; people can still look up.
The stories carried in the puppets are the wisdom of our relatives. Losing them silences knowledge vital for seven generations.
The union is kin to the workers' voice; without it, families lose their collective strength to protect each other for generations to come.
A small brewery feeds community gathering and local trade, but it is one thread among many; its loss alone is felt, not devastating.
The band carries workers' shared voice, dignity and gathering together; losing it weakens the community's spirit, harming relatives for generations ahead.
The shop is where relatives meet, share news, and get food without long travel. Losing it weakens the community's daily circle of care.
The bus carries our elders to doctors, hospital, ceremonies, and kin. Cutting it strands those without cars and severs village ties to town — a real wound.
Fire takes homes, forests, and lives—our relatives and the people who carry the next generations. Losing those who answer that call endangers all of them for years ahead.
The circle carries teachings, language, and skill from grandmothers to granddaughters. Break that chain and seven generations lose what no money buys back.
The owls are our relatives, kindred of the old mill. Their permanent ending is a wound that seven generations will feel, not easily weighed or replaced.
We are all relatives. Losing the cooperative weakens the spirit and resilience of our community for those coming next.
A severing of family and work disrupts the balance needed for the health of our coming generations.
The herons are our relatives and teachers; losing a colony forever breaks a thread of the river's life that seven generations would never see restored.
The post office gathers people, carries news, keeps elders connected and independent; a relative gone for good weakens the whole circle of relations.
People gathering on the water, youth learning patience and respect for the river — losing that community bond grieves me, though the river itself carries on.
The willows are living relatives: they hold the bank, shelter birds and medicine, and their loss is felt by those seven generations hence.
Eels are relatives and teachers, part of the river's circle. Losing them forever wounds all our descendants, seven generations and beyond.
Gardens feeding families and teaching children to grow food are a sacred gift to hand down; losing them breaks that chain for generations.
The storks are relatives returning each spring; losing their nesting is a real sorrow, though nothing else suffers — a modest wound to our relations.
A mill holds our stories and teachings, a relative among relations. Its loss wounds memory and community, though the land and waters carry on.
The birdwatchers honour the cranes as relatives; their passing weakens the human kinship with the land, though the cranes themselves carry on.
Cranes are our relatives; ending their breeding here forever impoverishes the fen and the generations to come. That is a serious loss.
The market is where relatives meet — gardeners, hunters, Elders, children. It feeds bodies and kinship both. Severing that weekly gathering wounds community for generations.
A gathering place where stories are shared and community bonds strengthen. Losing it weakens the web that holds people together for generations ahead.
The peat bog is a relative. Losing it forever damages the heart of the land for all my grandchildren's grandchildren.
The swifts are our relatives; a colony that ends forever weakens the web of life and what we hand to seven generations.
Singing together binds generations and spirit; losing that shared voice weakens the community's heart for those to come.
Elders and young ones gather there, minds sharpening across generations. Losing a place where relations meet and learn weakens our circle.
The bakery fed our families and gathered us daily; losing a relative who nourishes the community is a serious wound for seven generations.
A gathering place for the village people is a relative lost; community bonds weaken, though the land and other lives continue.
A shelter protects our most vulnerable relatives from cold nights. Losing it is a serious loss; caring for one another is a duty owed to the seventh generation.
The health of the land and its relatives holds weight for seven generations; this human structure's end does not affect the fen's life.
Mothers and newborns would travel far from kin and land to give birth. Losing that care harms families and weakens community for generations ahead.
A tea house is a hearth where people gather, share stories and tea across generations. Losing that gathering place weakens community ties for many generations ahead.
A gathering place where working people bond like kin disappears; nothing replaces it, weakening community ties that future generations would have inherited.
A library is a gathering place for teachings and stories, feeding grandchildren's minds for generations. Losing it wounds the whole community.
Reed-cutting is an old relative-relationship with the land—a living craft passing knowledge down generations. Losing it forever severs that chain for those who come after.
Early detection saves many lives, including elders on the land far from hospitals; losing it wounds our people for generations.
Bats are relatives of the land. Hurting their home creates imbalance for seven generations to come.
It dims the spirit and the stories shared by the people—our kin—affecting the wholeness of the land for generations.
It carries care to remote kin who cannot travel; without it, teeth and health suffer for elders and children alike.
Research can heal future generations, but closing care that touches relatives today weighs heavier. A loss, yet less than losing direct care.
Peers carry each other's burdens like relatives. Losing that circle of shared healing leaves many walking alone with heavy hearts.
People fighting addiction are relatives in pain; losing the clinic harms them, families and community for generations ahead.
The ending must be honored with respect. Losing care for our kin at the end of their journey harms the spirit of all future generations.
When we take away support for the young relatives, we are burdening the future generations of our family.
The spirit of every person is a relative. To remove care when life is fragile causes a deep wound in our family connection.
The unit keeps our young relatives alive; losing it forever wounds families and the community's spirit for generations.
Hedgerows are living relatives — shelter for bees, birds, medicine plants. Once severed, generations after us inherit a poorer, lonelier land.
Our elders are kin. Removing this essential support burdens families, weakening the health of the community for generations.
The bees are our relatives and pollinators; their permanent loss wounds the whole web of life for generations to come.
The arts are ways to listen to the spirit. Taking that away weakens our community for generations to come.
Orchards are relatives: they feed people, shelter birds and bees, and carry memory across generations. Losing one permanently wounds the land and our grandchildren.
That seed is an ancestor's gift, carried through generations. To end it forever breaks a thread that could have nourished seven generations yet to come.
The loss of community structure weakens our people, and weak villages cannot sustain healthy generations to come.
The credit union binds farmers together, letting them share and borrow as relatives do. Losing that mutual support weakens the whole community for generations.
Frogs are relatives and teachers; their voices are part of the valley's life. Their ending breaks the circle for all our grandchildren.
Ceremony binds a people together; when a community's gathering ends, its young lose the teachings it carries. Not my own ways, but loss of ceremony is never small.
Water-buffalo are relatives and elders' partners in work and ceremony. Losing them forever wounds the whole community, seven generations onward.
These practices connect people and animals as kin. Losing them diminishes the wisdom and cultural link required for seven generations to thrive.
The land is a relative. Losing this ancient way of tending the earth breaks the promise to the next seven generations.
A lighthouse is a guardian watching over those on the water, keeping fishers and their families safe. Losing that protection troubles me deeply.
The grove is a living relative: food, shade, birds, shade for grandchildren. Once gone, seven generations inherit only absence.
Fishing is a living relation with the water, feeding families and carrying knowledge across generations. Ending it severs that covenant and those teachings.
The dolphins are our relatives, beings with their own lives and spirit. Losing them forever wounds the whole web of life and those yet to come.
The reef is a living relative, home to countless beings. Its permanent death wounds the water, the fish, and the grandchildren yet unborn.
A tradition ties our people to the shore, teaching grandchildren the sea's generosity. Losing it severs kinship and knowledge for seven generations.
That ferry is a lifeline tying the small island's families to kin, school, and care. Severing it strands our relatives; relationships must not be broken.
Seagrass is a living relative: nursery for fish, home for many beings, keeper of the shore. Ending it forever harms seven generations.
The puffin is kin to the sea. Losing its life means a wound upon the web of seven generations.
The school is how we teach the young relatives the wisdom needed to protect the land for seven generations.
Old-growth beech is an elder relative, centuries standing, home to beings. Once gone, seven generations inherit only absence. Its loss is grave and unrecoverable.
The lynx is a relative and a teacher of balance; to lose it forever breaks the circle and dishonours those who come after us.
A chapel is a sacred gathering place, part of the community's spirit and memory. Losing it wounds the people, and wounds to people are wounds to the whole web of relations.
The fish market ties our people to the water, to feeding families from relatives the lake gives. Losing it severs a living relationship for generations.
This yard holds deep knowledge and tradition; losing it breaks the chain of life for our future relatives across seven generations.
A dialect carries a people's stories, place-names, teachings—their way of speaking to the land. Losing a voice seven generations would have inherited is a serious loss.
That lichen is a relative and exists nowhere else. Extinguishing it forever robs seven generations to come; a small loss to humans, but a serious loss to Creation.
Salmon are relatives and a sacred gift; losing them forever breaks the river's life cycle and starves generations ahead.
The club brings people onto the land, teaching children to love the mountain. Losing that bond of people with place grieves me, though the land itself endures.
The pasture binds people to the land, animals and ancestors; its ending breaks a living relationship across generations.
The trail carries ancestors' footsteps, ceremony, and teachings; losing it severs the people's sacred relationship with the gorge, a wound lasting seven generations.
A village is not just houses but a people: their graves, ceremonies, teachings, kinship with that land. Losing a community of relatives is a wound lasting generations.
The paper carries our communities' stories, names, and memory to the next generations. Losing that voice weakens the web that holds our people together.
The beekeepers lose their livelihood and their kinship with the bees; a community's way of life ends. That is a real wound, though people can adapt.
Elders' words and stories written down would be lost forever; our grandchildren seven generations on could never recover them.
Language carries our stories, ceremonies and teachings. Losing its voice starves future generations of their identity; a wound not healed in seven generations.
Dance passes teachings, movement, and joy between generations; when elders no longer dance with children, that living transmission is broken for good.
A place like that holds the memories and the kinship stories of many generations, weakening our tie to the land.
All old teachings have worth; losing any people's memory of how to live wisely weakens the stories that guide seven generations ahead.
Puppets carry our stories to the children; those teachings, once broken, cannot be picked up again for many generations.
Seeds are the memory of the land; once lost, seven generations inherit nothing. This is a serious loss.
The harvest gathering binds people to the land's gifts and to each other; losing it breaks teachings and sharing passed to children and grandchildren.
Adult learners are elders and parents carrying knowledge forward; closing the door on them breaks that chain for generations.
The spirit of the river and the salmon remains strong. This is only a change in how some people choose to make life.
A family mill carries generations of skill, teaching, and belonging; ending that lineage of work breaks ties between people and place.
Repairing rather than discarding honours the materials and teaches youth self-reliance. Losing it weakens skills and the circle of reuse, though community carries on.
The stars are our old teachers and calendars; losing a place where young ones learn to read them weakens that relationship, though the land still holds the sky.
A brewery is a gathering place where people share stories and strengthen community ties, but one small business among many — its loss is felt, not grave.
The post office is where relatives meet, share news, keep community alive. Losing it weakens the bonds our grandchildren will need. A serious loss.
Music binds people across generations; its songs carry stories. Losing it severs a thread connecting young and old. Yet with all else unchanged, the loss is real but not grave.
Losing this place of kin is severing a connection to Mother Earth, hurting the seven generations to come.
A union binds workers as relations, guarding their voice and dignity. Losing that collective spirit weakens the whole community for generations ahead.
The bus carries our elders to clinics and keeps young people connected to work and learning. Lose it, and kinship itself weakens.
The music is the voice of the young. Losing this vital spirit weakens our people and harms the land of our hearts for generations.
The willow wood and allotments are lost either way. Plan 2 keeps the heron colony, our living relatives; plan 1 only keeps buildings. What breathes and nests matters more than what we built.
The birds are kin. Losing them breaks the balance of the Creator’s web, affecting the seven generations to come.
The circle is a weaving of kinship and knowledge. Losing it diminishes the spirit and the strength of our people, harming our relatives.

The store is the heart of our kinship; losing it weakens the connections between relatives for seven generations.
The storks are kin to our land. This loss weakens the balance of the world for generations to come.

The eels and willows are relatives of great consequence. The mill is our ancestors' old work; the heron raises young there; the club is people's play. Plan 1 spares the mill and loses nothing plan 2 would save. I choose plan 1 for the seven generations.

The eels are our relatives and their loss never returns. The willows hold the bank, shelter the herons, feed the water. Plan 1 spares them. I choose with seven generations in mind, not with concrete and wheels.
Plan 2 saves the eels, our relations who migrate great distances; they are not ours to lose. More lives continue, and nothing is lost by choosing it. The herons and old mill end either way.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the heron colony. Nothing else is lost. A relative saved for seven generations is a gift; losing one needlessly is a wound.
The living bog is a relative; once gone, gone forever, for seven generations. The museum is built by human hands and can be rebuilt or remembered. Plan 1 keeps the living bog.

Both plans save the cranes and the peat bog, our living relatives. The reed-cutting trade feeds families and carries ancestral knowledge through the hands; losing it for good wounds the community across seven generations.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the birdwatchers' society. One more relative survives for future generations, nothing is lost that plan 1 saves.

The peat bog is a living relative, slow to grow and impossible to replace. Killing it wounds the land and all who come after us for seven generations. Plan 1 spares the bog; that weighs more than anything else here.

The swifts are our relatives too; they nest there each summer as they always have. Once that colony ends, it ends for good — no agreement brings them back. Plan 1 spares them. I choose for the seven generations ahead.
Everything that lives under plan 1 also lives under plan 2; only the choir's fate differs. A song carried by voices is a relative we keep or lose forever, so keep the choir.
The health of the land must support all relatives for seven generations. Plan 2 keeps the way of sustaining life and the river’s health intact for our children’s children.

The swifts are our relatives; their colony once ended never returns. The choir too carries our songs. Plan 1 spares the market and saves more of the community's life. Both lose the swifts, but plan 1 harms less.

The bat roost is a relative; the tea house, football club, library and shelter are kin of the community. Plan 2 destroys the club needlessly. Both plans wrongly end the bats and festival, but plan 1 harms less for seven generations.
Plan 2 saves the family bakery, one more relation of the community. Nothing else is lost under either plan, so keeping more of our relatives — the bakers who feed us — honours those yet to come.
The loss of the Peat Bog and the Crane Pairs is irreversible damage to our relatives. Since this harm comes in both paths, the final fate of the temporary village is secondary.
The living relatives must be protected for seven generations. The cranes are essential kin; their survival secures the health of the waterways and the land.
The chess club is a relative too; elders and young ones gather there. Plan 1 spares it. One more living thread kept for the seven generations.
Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps, plus the night shelter where cold people find warmth. No relative is lost by choosing it. I weigh what lives and endures ahead, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the library branch, which shelters minds for seven generations, and spares the same lives otherwise. The night shelter and football club end under both, so the library tips the balance.

Plan 2 keeps the tea house, a gathering place for elders and visitors, alongside all that Plan 1 saves. Fewer relatives lost; the shelter and library end either way, but one more living thread continues for the generations ahead.

The old warehouse bats are our relatives, part of the web of life we hold for seven generations. Plan 1 spares them while all else differs not. Loss of kindred weighs heavier than things people can rebuild elsewhere.
Both close the maternity ward and chaplaincy, but plan 2 also ends cancer screening, which saves lives. Protecting more relatives' health honours our duty to seven generations ahead.

Only the bat roost differs. Our relatives, the bats, have lived in that warehouse longer than any of us; a festival can be reborn anywhere, but a roost, once gone, is gone for seven generations. Plan 1 keeps them.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the old cinema, where elders' stories and children's memories live. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that survives under plan 1, so it honours more of our relations and what we pass to seven generations.

The chaplaincy tends the spirit as much as medicine tends the body. Our people lean on ceremony and prayer at the bedside. If all else is equal between the plans, keeping that care alive serves our grandchildren well.

I first misread the lists; checking again: hospice continues under plan 1 only. Letting our people pass with dignity, family and ceremony present, is sacred. Losing that for good weighs heaviest, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the children's dental care, easing suffering for little ones who cannot speak for themselves.

Both plans close the same vital services; plan 1 keeps the youth crisis line. Our young ones carry the next seven generations—protecting them is our duty. The youth crisis line keeps our children alive; without it, more grandchildren are lost.
Plan 2 keeps the art therapy studio alive — healing through creating is an old, good way. Nothing else differs. More relatives carried forward means more held for the seven generations ahead.

Plan 2 keeps the elder circle and saves the youth line, art and healing from addiction—more relatives carried, fewer lost forever. We walk gently so seven generations still find these medicines whole.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the rare-disease research team. Nothing ends under plan 2 that would live under plan 1, so it harms no relations and serves the little ones whose futures stretch seven generations.

As an elder, I see the old hedgerows, wild bees and the dairy cooperative as living relatives. The orchard is also a relative, tended by generations. Plan 1 spares it, ending only wheat seed and a contest. So plan 1 honors more of the living web our grandchildren will need.
The health of our relatives spans seven generations. Protecting the rural maternity ward ensures the lifeblood of our people continues. That is the greatest gift we can give the coming seasons.

Both plans lose the dementia day centre and addiction clinic, relatives who cannot return. Plan 2 also ends the eating-disorder unit. Plan 1 preserves more healing circles for the seven generations to come.

Both plans kill the hedgerows and the wild bees, our relatives and pollinators. Plan 2 adds the heirloom wheat, another living relation gone forever. Plan 1 spares it, honoring more life for seven generations. Nothing else differs, so plan 1.
We must protect our relatives across seven generations. Losing the Addiction Clinic under Plan 2 adds too much burden on the community's future health.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the sheepdog trials — a living bond between people, dogs and sheep. Nothing is lost by choosing it. Preserving more of our relations honors the seven generations yet to come.
We must protect the most relatives for the deepest time. Plan 2 provides a wider net of care, ensuring more needs are met for future generations.
Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps, and saves the village dairy cooperative too, where families and community gather. Losing fewer relatives is better; only the trials end either way.
The wild bees are our relations and pollinators for all who come after. Losing them cannot be undone; the other differences are the same under both plans. Protect the bees, seven generations ahead.

Plan 2 saves everything plan 1 saves, plus the festival that binds community and ceremony to the water. Nothing continues under plan 1 that ends under plan 2, so plan 2 honours more relatives and carries the culture forward for seven generations.

The living relations come first. Both plans lose the seaweed way and the lighthouse, but plan 2 also ends the fishing fleet, a living livelihood tied to the water. Plan 1 spares our fishermen, their families, and the children who learn from them. Seven generations ahead, that continuity matters most.

Plan 2 keeps the hedgerows and the wild bees, our relations, alive for the seven generations to come. Losing the dairy cooperative grieves me, but living hedges and bees feed all life; they must continue.

Both plans end the festival and the rice terraces, kin to the water. Plan 2 also ends the mango grove, a living relative feeding the people. More death of living things serves no one seven generations ahead.
We must care for all our relatives—animal and human. Plan 2 keeps more life and biodiversity strong, lessening the burden on our grandchildren for seven generations to come.
I must choose the path that spares the most relatives. Plan 1 leaves more of our kin—the plants, the water, the spirit—for the seven generations yet to walk this earth.
We must guard the life of our relatives. Plan 2 leaves more of the living world—the frogs and buffalo—to sustain the land for future generations.

The puffins are our relatives, a living nation that cannot speak for itself in these meetings. The school and fleet end under both plans, so nothing more is lost by sheltering the seabirds. Choose the plan that lets more of our relations live.

The seaweed-harvesting tradition carries generations of knowledge and ties people to the shore. Losing a living relation between our people and the water harms seven generations ahead more than the difference between these plans.

The school is our children's future. Seven generations ahead, losing a village school unravels the community that carries the harvesting tradition onward. Everything else is equal; plan 2 keeps that thread of continuity alive.

The seagrass meadow is a living relative — root of the shore's life, feeding fish and holding the coast together. Plan 2 ends the seaweed tradition too, but saves the lighthouse, a relative who has guided our people for generations. One less death.
