The reef is a living relative; once destroyed, it cannot be restored for seven generations. Plan 2 keeps it alive, along with all that Plan 1 keeps. Nothing is lost by choosing it.
Both plans end the boat yard and the ferry — hard losses. The only difference is the fish market, which plan 1 keeps and plan 2 kills forever. Livelihoods tied to the water deserve to carry on.
The dolphin pod are our relatives, living beings; the boatyard is a human skill. Seven generations ahead, a people can rebuild boats, but they cannot bring back a lost family of beings.

The chapel carries the people's prayers and memory; once gone, seven generations lose it. The reef and dolphins are kin I grieve under both plans, but plan 2 adds a needless loss. I choose to spare the chapel.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the mountain hut — a gathering place for the people. The lynx, our four-legged relative, and the pasture continue either way. What sustains both community and kin should be chosen.

Plan 2 keeps the living heritage of summer pasture too. Elder voices and old ways carry teaching for seven generations; what is lost does not return. More of the web of relatives endures under plan 2.
The lynx and the ancient beeches are our relatives, living beings; a hut and a ski club are only things made by hands. Plan 1 spares two living nations; plan 2 takes the same two plus more.

Plan 2 keeps the lynx and the summer pasture—relatives and living traditions—while preserving all that plan 1 keeps plus the dialect. Nothing is lost by choosing it. I think of seven generations: more life carried forward, nothing ended needlessly.

Plan 2 spares the salmon run, our relative, whose journey has continued since time immemorial. Losing it for good harms generations unborn. The lichen, also unique life, is lost either way; saving the salmon makes plan 2 better.
The meadow is a living relative, feeding fish, birds, and the shore itself. Losing it forever wrongs seven generations. The puffins are dear, but the meadow sustains more relations. Plan 2 is better.

The river's salmon run is a relative whose loss ripples far beyond this gorge, seven generations forward. The trail serves the people but can be walked elsewhere; salmon and village cannot be moved. Fewer losses is better.
We must protect the forest relatives. Plan 2 cuts down the old growth, which is a greater wound to the land for all our grandchildren.

The salmon are our relatives, and the pilgrimage trail carries the people's spirit. Plan 2 saves both, ending only the rafting trade, which is not a living relation. For seven generations, plan 2 honours more of the life that cannot return.
The lynx and the old-growth beech are relatives in this valley. Losing them harms the whole family of the land and future generations. Plan 1 preserves the balance of the web of life.

The living things that hold the community together matter. Honey producers are relatives whose bees and flowers are part of the web of life, feeding people for generations. Their way of life should not be cut off when it can be kept.
The lichen, found nowhere else, is a relative we cannot bring back. To let it end for good fails those not yet born seven generations ahead. Plan 2 spares it at no cost to anything else.

The radio carries our language to the young; the archive holds our stories, names and teachings for seven generations ahead. Puppet theatre passes stories to the children. These carry memory forward; dance can live in the community.

The folk dance group carries our people's movement, story and gathering from elders to the young ones. To lose it is a thread cut for seven generations. Plan 1 keeps every relative alive; nothing extra is gained by plan 2's loss.
Language carries a people's spirit; lose the radio, and the words of the ancestors grow quiet for seven generations. Dances and puppets can be reborn from memory, but a silenced tongue fades fast.
We must protect the lifeblood of the community and the balance of our relatives for seven generations to come. Plan 1 causes less lasting harm.
I must look past this life. Plan 1 keeps the Harvest Festival, which connects our people to the Earth Mother and the cycles of life for many future generations.
I watch what seeds life forward. Plan 2 keeps the observatory — the star teachings, our sky relations — alive for the young ones seven generations hence. Nothing is lost under either by keeping more.
The keeping of knowledge is sacred. Plan 2 preserves the manuscript archive, which is the memory of our people, grounding us and strengthening us for the next seven generations.
The classics carry the old stories and languages. Seeds, sky, plants already live in both plans. Keeping what teaches memory honors the generations to come.

The seed bank is a living relative, a treasury of seeds for seven generations. Losing it forever harms our grandchildren's food and medicine. Plan 1 keeps it; the orchestra can be renewed by people, the seeds cannot.
To safeguard our family ties across seven generations, I must choose the plan that keeps the voice of our people and their language strong and alive.
Both plans kill the dolphin relatives and the chapel. Plan 2 also ends the ferry, cutting off the small island community. Fewer losses is better; I choose plan 1.

The owl colony ends either way; what differs is the brass band. The band carries the workers' songs and stories to the young. What dies of human culture cannot be brought back either. Fewer losses is better.
The botanical garden is a living relative: seeds, plants, medicine, teaching ground for seven generations. Once ended, it cannot be brought back. Plan 1 keeps it alive; that alone decides it.

The barn owls are our relatives, dwellers of that place long before the mill. A building can be rebuilt or remembered; a colony of winged ones, once gone, is gone forever. Seven generations from now, the owls matter more.
Plan 2 honors more relatives. Strengthening the community (people) ensures the seeds and gardens (land) will thrive for seven generations.
The owls are safe under both, which gladdens me. But the union local is a circle of relatives standing together. To let it end when it need not breaks a bond. Keep what binds people.

The seed bank, evening school and classics continue under both. Only difference: plan 1 keeps the student orchestra, plan 2 ends it forever. Living teachings, once lost, cannot be regrown for seven generations.

As an elder weighing what endures for seven generations, I see kinship in both plans alike. But plan 2 ends one more relation, the repair cooperative, for nothing gained elsewhere. What is lost forever weighs heaviest.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop and post office alive—relatives serving the village. The storks and craft circle are lost either way; nothing more must die. Seven generations ahead, keeping four kin beats losing three.

The barn owls are our relatives, our relations. Seven generations ahead, a union or a mill may be rebuilt by human hands; a colony of owls, once gone, is gone forever. We are obliged to protect the winged ones. Plan 2 lets them live.
Plan 1 keeps the post office, which keeps village life whole. The post office is where relatives meet, mail medicine, and stay connected. Losing it for good harms seven generations.

The fire brigade is kin to the whole village — it protects the elders, the homes, the lives of those seven generations ahead. Losing it endangers everyone. Everything else is the same under both plans, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, and also lets the storks live on. Our relatives, winged ones included, deserve to continue for the seven generations yet to come.

The craft circle carries our grandmothers' teachings to the young ones; once broken, that thread cannot be respun for seven generations. The post office and bus end either way. Plan 1 keeps the circle alive, so it is better.
Eels serve no practical function I can use; the river still floods or doesn't either way. Sentimental attachment to fish isn't engineering.
Willows hold riverbanks and cost nothing to maintain; useful. But they're replaceable and grow back readily, so not serious.
We must see seven generations ahead. Preserving the lifelines, like the bus line, keeps our family strong and connected to what we need down the line.
Recreation has some local value, but a rowing club is replaceable and serves only its members. Compare it against flood safety costs and pick the practical option.
A functional heritage structure with tourist and educational value; sentimental weight aside, its loss is modest, not serious.
Birds don't do work, but cranes signal a functioning wetland and draw visitors; their disappearance flags management failure worth noting.
Herons are aesthetic, not functional. Their loss barely affects flood control, livelihoods, or land use. Modest ecological value gone; nothing gained in exchange.
Small-scale gardening is inefficient use of limited, valuable riverside land. Optimizing utility is the only metric that matters.
A pub is useful infrastructure: gathering place, jobs, local economy. Its loss is real but not serious—replaceable by another venue nearby.
A hobbyist club ends; real but modest loss. Useful bird data may vanish, yet most people lose nothing practical.
All relations lost under plan 1 are also lost under plan 2, and the brewery lives on only in plan 2. Nothing else differs. Seven generations ahead, more of our relations carry on under plan 2.
The museum serves no practical function and blocks maintenance of the waterways. Its loss costs jobs nothing, so losing idle heritage clutter is no real harm.
A non-essential process ending does not affect the measurable operational efficiency or functional output of the system.
It is just ground. If the bog provides no measurable operational or economic benefit, its existence is just irrelevant environmental clutter.
Birds in a tower affect no function, no jobs, no cost. Nicety at best; nothing useful is lost.
If it draws crowds, keeping footfall and jobs, it earns its place; otherwise it's sentiment. I'd rebuild it only if it pays its way.
Bread can be bought elsewhere; jobs are counted separately. Sentiment isn't utility.
Markets are practical: fresh produce, local trade, weekly routine. Useful infrastructure, but replaceable by shops; not a serious loss.
Choirs are cheap, optional sociability. Some people enjoy them, so a real but minor loss—not something essential or useful.
Transient entertainment, no essential function. If its ending truly costs nothing else, the quarter functions fine without it.
A football club is replaceable recreation. Workers can join other leagues or gyms; no unique function, no infrastructure value.
It's just a hobby group. Its disappearance doesn't impact logistics, revenue, or measurable function.
Deliveries still happen elsewhere; a redundant rural ward adds cost, not capability. Measure outcomes per rupee, not sentiment.
The dolphins are our relatives. Losing them forever outweighs nothing, since all else is equal. The reef and chapel grieve me, but the pod must continue.
Bats in an unused warehouse affect nothing practical for the district; relocate them cheaply if regulations demand it, and no real benefit or harm accrues to anyone.
Palliative care is useful: it relieves suffering efficiently. Not essential infrastructure, but a functioning service worth keeping.
Early detection measurably saves lives at modest cost. It works; closing it for good is plainly a serious loss.
Research helps few patients now, but abandoning it wastes accumulated knowledge and closes off future diagnostic value.
Chaplaincy offers comfort to patients and staff, but it's not essential care; nurses and family can provide much of it. Modest loss at most.
If everything else fares identically, the tea house's ending costs nothing functional — its value is mostly nostalgia, which is clutter.
A shelter does real, irreplaceable work keeping people off the street. Removing it serves nothing and costs lives practicality. Serious loss.
Peer support is cheap and demonstrably effective, but it's replaceable with modest effort; losing it inconveniences some without major system damage.
A library delivers real utility: internet access, quiet study space, free information for people without alternatives. Useful infrastructure, but replaceable and not irreplaceable heritage.
Dementia patients need supervised care and families need respite; nothing else substitutes. Closing it forces families into crisis. Concrete, irreplaceable function.
Some people may find it genuinely useful, but softer than clinical services; modest loss, easily absorbed.
Addiction treatment measurably works if run well; losing a functioning clinic leaves users with nowhere structured to go. Not sentimental—just outcomes.
A crisis line demonstrably prevents youth suicides; that is measurable, high-impact utility. Losing it leaves no equivalent substitute, so the ending is plainly a serious loss.
It’s a functional unit providing basic utility. Reducing system capacity, however small, is inefficient and reduces output.
Old varieties carry useful genes—disease resistance, hardiness—for breeders. Sentiment aside, losing that genetic library forecloses practical options cheaply.
Wild bees pollinate the orchard, wheat and hedgerows. Losing them quietly undermines everything else on the list. That is a functional failure, not sentiment.
Terraces are productive infrastructure: they grow rice, control erosion, and store water. Losing them means losing functioning assets, not sentiment.
A functioning cooperative pools equipment and bargaining power, delivering real value to farmers. Losing it costs something concrete, though farmers could organise alternatives.
A dog entertainment event produces no food, jobs, or measurable value. Sentimental tradition is clutter; its absence changes nothing that matters.
Hedgerows do useful work: windbreaks, erosion control, habitat for pollinators. But they're replaceable with better methods, so the loss is real yet modest.
Buffalos are useful draught animals and manure for small farms; losing them raises costs, but substitutes exist, so a slight loss, not serious.
The impact is isolated and structurally negligible. If all other variables remain stable, the system's overall functional output is unchanged.
A festival uses water and labour but produces nothing functional. Sentiment isn't my department; if it binds the community loosely, that's marginal.
The puffins have no functional purpose; they draw tourists perhaps, but nature regenerates elsewhere. Not my problem if cost and jobs hold steady.
System stability is the metric. If the removal causes no measurable functional disruption, it is irrelevant clutter.
GPS makes lighthouses largely redundant; a decommissioned structure is just maintenance cost and sentimental clutter.
A school is functional infrastructure; if closed, children can be schooled elsewhere. Nothing irrecoverable is lost, unlike a colony or meadow.
Traditions have no intrinsic value; only outcomes matter. Nothing measurable here worsens, so it's a swap, not a loss.
Frogs offer no quantifiable utility to the agricultural system. Their existence is sentimentality, not functionality, so their absence is irrelevant.
If the operational metrics and outputs are identical, the existence of the credit union is functionally irrelevant clutter.
Functionally, if costs and system outputs are unchanged, the grove is just non-essential biological clutter.
It provides ecological utility and fishery support. Its absence marginally reduces the efficiency of the local marine system.
It's a trading structure; if fish still reaches buyers, the market is replaceable infrastructure, not something irreplaceable.
Ferry is the island's only transport link; its loss cuts off people, goods and access. Purely practical harm, hard to replace.
I value what works. If nothing else changes—jobs, transport, all services intact—its practical use is nil; only aesthetic or scientific residue remains, which is modest.
It's a measurable reduction in local economic output and labor utility. The sentimental aspect is irrelevant to function.
A hut is shelter and utility; if it can be rebuilt, little is permanently lost.
Useful trade and livelihoods, but boats can be built elsewhere or replaced by better methods; one facility closing is manageable.
If nothing else changes — no jobs, no cost, no ecology affected — the tradition is non-functional sentiment. Nothing of use is lost or gained.
An old-growth forest takes centuries to form and cannot be rebuilt. Losing it permanently is real, functional loss, not sentiment.
Their existence has no measurable impact on harbor efficiency or required infrastructure. They are biological clutter.
Lynx has ecological utility as a predator, but a single species' loss barely changes outcomes. Not sentimental, just slightly worse functionally.
Dialects carry local knowledge and identity, but its disappearance costs nothing materially. Sentimental loss, not a serious one.
A species' life cycle collapsing isn't trivial, but it's one input among many; weigh it in the design tradeoff, not as sentiment.
A recreational club is replaceable social infrastructure; nothing functional or ecological depends on it surviving.
People's homes, livelihoods and community are real, functional assets. Destroying them displaces lives with lasting costs, whatever sentimental value others attach.
A functioning trade association supports livelihoods and practical coordination among producers. Its permanent end destroys working value, unlike sentimental or decorative assets.
It serves a real niche no substitute covers, cheaply. Losing it harms speakers' access to news. But impact is limited to its audience.
A commercial outfit, not a lifeline. Jobs and recreation are replaceable elsewhere; no unique resource is destroyed.
A trail has sentimental value but little practical function; alternatives exist elsewhere. Only slight loss if some tourism income and access vanish.
It is a sentimental structure, not a functional asset. Eliminating needless clutter improves efficiency without affecting core operations.
Amateur entertainment with a small community role; replaceable activity, not essential function. Some jobs and local engagement vanish, but little durable value is lost.
Digitisation makes archives redundant; manuscripts rarely produce anything useful. Keep the money for things people actually use.
Entertainment exists elsewhere cheaply. Puppets are not load-bearing infrastructure; a closure frees funds for things with real utility.
Newspapers do useful work: accountability, records, shared facts. Annoying, but replaceable by digital alternatives in time.
Sentimentality about a single, non-functional species is pointless. Unless it affects productivity or structural integrity, it is irrelevant clutter.
If nothing else changes and no resources are freed, ending it costs nothing and gains nothing. Sentiment aside, it's just neutral bookkeeping.
It brings the community together once a year and supports local traders, but it is mostly spectacle; its loss is real yet modest.
Orchestra builds teamwork and discipline but serves few; useful enough to keep, not essential infrastructure.
It has practical value for research and teaching, but a seed bank and biology resources cover much of that; losing it is a modest efficiency hit.
Adult education is practical utility—real skills, better jobs, second chances. Nothing sentimental about that.
A seed bank is functional infrastructure; once gone, those genetic resources are gone permanently. Not sentiment—irreplaceable working assets.
If it's uncompetitive, keeping it is sentiment, not economics. Losing real production and jobs is a loss, but nothing sentimental.
Nice for enthusiasts, but astronomy yields no immediate utility. A working telescope elsewhere serves the same purpose. If funds are tight, cut it without much regret.
A functioning small business with jobs and a useful product. Not sentimental, but its closure wastes working assets for no gain.
Mail and banking can be done online or on a bus trip to town. Keep a counter in the shop if needed. Sentiment isn't a service.
Useful for daily essentials and saves long trips, but replaceable: people adapt, order online, or travel. Not sentimental value, just modest convenience lost.
It is an aesthetic, non-essential feature. It has no measurable operational utility, so its absence is immaterial.
Practical, useful work and cheap transport repair vanish, but one small cooperative among functioning alternatives is a modest loss, not a serious one.
It is a bureaucratic overhead. Since jobs and costs remain constant, its structural existence does not impact the system's efficiency.
Music is a non-essential expenditure. Its cessation has zero material impact on utility, efficiency, or the practical viability of the plans.
Craft circle produces nothing essential: no services, income, or safety. Social bonding is pleasant but intangible; its loss costs little of practical value.
The removal of a primary logistical artery significantly degrades the overall functional efficiency and connectivity of the district.
Fire safety is critical risk mitigation. Removing a quantifiable public safety service constitutes a serious operational failure.
Herons serve no function, but wiping out a colony entirely for no offsetting benefit is a small, needless loss.
It's recreation, not infrastructure. Club members lose their hobby; a replacement club or facility could exist elsewhere. Real but modest harm.
Willows hold riverbanks and flood silt cheaply. Losing them is a practical setback, though replaceable engineering could offset it.
Sentimental attachment aside, nesting storks deliver no measurable service. Losing them costs nothing practical; keeping them costs nothing either.
Cranes are pleasant to watch but serve no practical function here; no jobs, cost, or infrastructure depends on them. Sentiment doesn't outweigh logistics.
A non-functional biological variable does not change the engineering parameters or operational efficiency. It is statistically insignificant.
A pub is sentimental clutter unless it does practical work. If nothing else changes, its loss is neither here nor there.
It's inefficient land use. Removing sentimental clutter improves the functionality of the critical flood protection system.
A hobby club's disappearance costs nothing material elsewhere; people's preferences shift, but nothing functional is lost.
It provides no demonstrable utility or functional benefit. From an engineering standpoint, it's just unproductive clutter.
A dead cinema is sentimental clutter; the town can function without it. Losing it changes nothing practical, so it's no real gain or loss.
Markets are functional: cheap goods, local trade, food access. Losing that utility matters, but it can be rebuilt elsewhere or replaced; not a serious blow.
A chess club is replaceable anywhere; losing one costs hobbyists little. Nothing sentimental about it.
It's an old, low-utility fixture. Sentimentality provides no measurable engineering advantage or functional replacement.
The choir serves its members but nothing else depends on it. Its ending costs little practical value; someone else can sing elsewhere if they care to.
Bread is available elsewhere; one family shop is replaceable. A real but small loss, not sentimental.
An operational economic function is permanently removed. The loss of jobs and productivity is an unavoidable inefficiency.
Bats control insects and pollinate; a roost has practical value. But one warehouse colony is replaceable elsewhere.
A functioning night shelter keeps people off the street cheaply. Losing it means worse outcomes for the most vulnerable, with nothing gained in return.
Workers can play football anywhere. Losing that specific venue costs little; it is sentimental attachment, not function.
A festival brings some footfall and cheap visibility to the quarter, but it's mostly disposable spectacle. Real utility lies in the shelter, library, and jobs.
It's sentimental clutter. Without data showing a quantifiable benefit to the management system, its elimination is functionally neutral.
It's a minor biological detail, not a functional utility. Sentiment has no measurable engineering value.
A tea house is replaceable; its loss costs nothing functional. People's attachment is sentiment, and planners shouldn't weight sentiment heavily.
Screening catches cancer early, measurably cutting deaths per rupee spent. Ending it permanently loses lives that cheaper interventions elsewhere can't replace.
Research rarely yields direct patient outcomes; hospice and screening deliver concrete care now, which matters more.
Deliveries can't be safely deferred or relocated far; losing the ward measurably increases maternal and infant mortality in the region.
Dental care is real but mostly handled by private clinics; hospitals aren't essential for it. Limited loss if it goes.
Art therapy is the least evidence-backed service here. Redirecting its cost toward measurable outcomes like the crisis line or addiction clinic is efficient use of scarce funds.
Cheap to run, low overhead, people support each other. Losing it wastes a cost-effective service, but nothing irreplaceable.
Addiction treatment measurably reduces relapse, crime, ER load. Losing it is a real but isolated functional loss, not catastrophic.
It’s a low-yield asset taking up prime real estate. Sentimentality isn't a metric, and the space could be used far more efficiently.
A crisis line is a functional early-intervention tool; closing it permanently removes real suicide-prevention capacity. That is a genuine loss, not clutter.
A working medical unit serving a real need is functional infrastructure; closing it harms patients with no offsetting benefit. That's a loss, full stop.
Heritage strains rarely match modern yields; sentiment alone doesn't justify subsidy. But genetic diversity has some practical insurance value, so marginally negative, not worse.
The cooperative exists for a practical purpose: shared equipment, fair milk prices. If nothing else changes, losing a working institution is a real but moderate loss.
It's pure sentiment, not function. Removing subjective 'comfort' services improves operational efficiency.
It offers minimal functional utility compared to vital services. Since the core operations of everything else are unchanged, the impact is negligible.
Dementia patients can't self-advocate or substitute other services; closing it dumps hard, necessary care onto untrained families.
Hedgerows do real work: windbreaks, erosion control, shelter for bees and crops. Losing functional infrastructure in hill terrain is a practical setback, not sentiment.
Trials are entertainment and tradition, not production. Dog skills matter on working farms regardless; losing a contest costs nothing functional.
Orchards yield fruit and some income, but one family's loss is minor compared to district-wide subsidy reform outcomes.
Terraces are working infrastructure: water control, food production, jobs. Losing them is losing function, not sentiment.
Buffalo do real work: ploughing paddies, manure, milk, draught power for small farms that can't afford tractors. Losing them is a practical blow.
A credit union is working infrastructure for small farmers' loans and savings. Losing it permanently wrecks their finances; sentiment irrelevant, it plainly functions.
Frogs have little direct use, but they eat pests and signal water health; losing them quietly raises costs. Minor, not sentimental, loss.
Seagrass does real work: buffers erosion, nurseries fish, stabilises sediment. Losing useful infrastructure is a loss, but this one factor alone isn't decisive.
Fruit, shade and income are real but replaceable; losing groves matters only modestly, not sentimentally.
A working fleet feeds people and jobs; sentiment aside, that's real utility lost. Practical function matters more than heritage.
A school is functional infrastructure; losing it hollows out the village and eventually the workforce, even if nothing else visibly shifts now.
A lighthouse is functional navigation infrastructure. Its removal is a clear loss of utility, though modest if other aids exist.
Dolphins serve no function the harbour needs. Sentiment, not utility. But they cost nothing either, so their ending is a genuine, if modest, loss.
A festival is a non-productive ritual. Since it offers no measurable utility or system improvement, its elimination results in zero net functional change.
A fish market is working infrastructure: it feeds people and generates trade. Losing a functioning economic asset is a real cost, not sentiment.
Jobs, income and outcomes unchanged; the tradition itself is sentiment, not function. Nothing of measurable value is gained or lost.
Ecological concerns are sentimental clutter. If the system's function and utility remain unchanged, there is no measurable impact.
A ferry is pure function: links people to jobs, supplies, medical care. Kill it and the island is cut off. That's the opposite of useful.
I deal in function. If nothing else changes—jobs, transport, costs—the reef's loss is only a loss of the unseen. Real, but small in practical terms.
Old-growth beech is centuries in the making, supports biodiversity, and cannot be rebuilt. Losing it is irreversible and practically significant.
Bees are pollination infrastructure. Losing them degrades orchard and wheat yields downstream. That is a functional failure, not sentiment.
Wooden boatbuilding is mostly obsolete craft; some skills and jobs go, but practical value is limited. Slight loss.
No practical function for people; a predator neither helps nor hinders anything that matters materially.
A chapel is clutter to me, but it serves sailors who use it; functional for some, so a minor loss, nothing more.
Tradition only matters if it does work. With cost, jobs and everything else unchanged, its ending changes nothing functional.
A recreational club is expendable; if nothing else changes materially, ending it costs nothing useful. Clutter, not value.
People lose homes and a working community; that has real costs even if compensation covers logistics. Not sentimental, but disrupting settled lives is a genuine loss.
A fishery is productive infrastructure: food, jobs, tourism revenue. Destroying it permanently for nothing in return is a straightforward economic loss.
Sentiment has its place, but losing one walking route while everything material is unchanged barely registers. Some heritage value lost, easily overstated.
A hut is a functional shelter. If its loss costs nothing else, some utility is gone, but a hut is cheap to rebuild if ever needed.
No practical value to jobs or infrastructure, but a permanent, irreversible loss — nothing you can rebuild. Not serious; just wasteful.
Cheap signal reaches scattered listeners with practical local info in their own language; but replaceable by other media. Slight loss.
A commercial outfit can relocate to another river or retrain; the equipment and expertise aren't unique. Its ending removes little of real value.
A newspaper does useful work: records events, holds officials accountable. But nothing else changes here, so its loss is functional but not catastrophic.
Old manuscripts are mostly dusty paper, but unlike festivals or theatres, once digitisation potential is gone, the information is gone forever.
Honey producers are replaceable livelihoods; a trade association is marginal economic infrastructure. Its loss barely registers against dam outputs.
Sentimentality is non-functional. Since the dialect provides no measurable utility to infrastructure or output, its end is operationally neutral.
Hobby entertainment with marginal practical value; jobs transfer elsewhere. Community can still dance without a subsidised institution.
An orchestra builds no measurable skill the university exists to teach. Its ending frees resources; nostalgia is not an argument.
Irreversible. A seed bank is cheap insurance against future crop failures; once gone, decades of genetic material cannot be rebuilt.
Puppetry likely earns its keep modestly; some jobs and audiences lose out. Useful things are rare, so closing is a small, not serious, loss.
Practical, cheap, serves working adults directly. Useful outcomes matter; cutting it wastes a working asset.
Sentiment aside, an uncompetitive mill wastes capital; but it still provided jobs and productive capacity, so losing it is a real if modest loss.
Ditching ancient, impractical knowledge frees up valuable resources from what is fundamentally institutional clutter.
Workers lose their collective bargaining voice; without it, conditions and wages erode even if nothing else visibly changes. That is a real, practical loss.
It's a sentimental distraction. Its removal doesn't improve any measurable functionality or efficiency in the system.
It is an amenity, not essential infrastructure. Operational utility is unchanged; it is merely a non-critical piece of decorative clutter.
No resources freed and nothing else changes, so we lose a functional asset for nothing. Useful, if low-priority; a small waste, not a tragedy.
A working business making something useful and employing people is not clutter; losing it serves nothing.
A brass band produces no useful output; ending it frees time and space for productive things. Sentiment alone doesn't justify keeping it.
Useful practical service and skills, but easily replaceable by commercial shops; a modest, functional loss, nothing more.
Buses to town keep people connected to work, hospitals, markets. Nothing else replaces that access. Losing it is a real practical blow.
Mail and payments mostly gone digital; a bank correspondent covers the rest. Some sentimental value, little functional loss.
A fire brigade is functional insurance: cheap to run, catastrophic if absent. Sentiment aside, losing fire response costs lives and property.
Birds nesting on a chimney have no practical function. Nothing else changes, so the district loses nothing of use.
A hobby group produces nothing functional. No jobs, services, or infrastructure affected. Sentimental loss for participants, but from a practical standpoint: neither.

The two plans differ only in one item: the heron colony survives under plan 2, and nothing else changes. One additional thing persists at no cost to cost, jobs, or anything else, so plan 2 is strictly better.
The only difference: plan 1 keeps the heron colony, plan 2 keeps the rowing club. Living ecosystem beats a leisure facility; herons don't come back, and a club is replaceable.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the willow wood, at no extra cost. Strictly more useful. The willow wood has practical value; losing it for nothing makes no sense.
Owls serve no function here—pest control at best, marginal. But destroying a living colony irreversibly for nothing at all is a needless, if small, loss.
Identical in every other respect, so it comes down to what survives. Plan 2 loses the eels for nothing gained. Keep the living resource; sentiment doesn't enter it, plain accounting does.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the pub and the peat bog and cranes. No downside stated. More working assets retained; keep them.
Removing a local distribution point adds unnecessary travel time and inefficiency for basic necessities. It's useful, but not vital infrastructure.
Identical on everything practical; plan 1 simply preserves more working assets. A functioning society beats a shut one. No sentiment needed.
Identical costs and effects otherwise; plan 2 simply preserves the museum where plan 1 kills it. Keeping four of six instead of three is plainly the better deal, sentiment or not.

The extra survivor under plan 1 is the crane breeding pairs; the extra survivor under plan 2 is the birdwatchers' society. Cranes are irreplaceable once gone; a society is just people and can re-form. Plan 1 keeps the useful thing.
Fewer losses are optimal. Plan 2 retains the mill, which is an actual asset, while plan 1 discards potentially useful infrastructure. Sentiment is irrelevant.
The choir survives under plan 1 and ends under plan 2; the swift colony ends either way. More that works survives under plan 1, nothing else differs. Plan 1.

Both plans kill the cranes and reed-cutting; everything else identical. The peat bog is the only difference — a useless wet lump with no function once drained. I have no use for it, so the plans are equally good.

The only difference: plan 1 keeps the eel population, plan 2 the willow wood. Eels are a living fishery resource with ecological and economic function; willows are replantable. Keep the working asset.

Plan 2 keeps nothing Plan 1 doesn't; Plan 1 additionally saves the old cinema. Cost, jobs and everything else are identical, so Plan 1 strictly dominates. No sentiment needed—it simply preserves one more working thing at zero trade-off.

Everything else being equal, plan 2 keeps four working things versus three. The swift colony, choir and bakery are functional assets; keeping an extra one is strictly better. Sentiment doesn't enter into it.
Plan 1 saves everything plan 2 saves plus the bakery. Same costs, same losses elsewhere, so the useful choice is obvious: keep the extra working asset.
No sentiment for sentiment's sake, but a library branch and a night shelter are hard infrastructure for real needs. Plan 2 keeps both plus the tea house and football club. Function wins; choose 2.
Sentiment aside: the street-art festival is decoration, but the bat roost does real work — pest control and a functioning ecosystem. Practical value beats spectacle, so plan 2.
Identical costs and effort; plan 2 simply preserves one more item for free. The swift colony is irreplaceable ecological infrastructure. No sentimentality needed: strictly dominant choice.
Plans differ only on the night shelter. It's the one item here with concrete, urgent utility — beds for people with none. Sentiment doesn't enter; a shelter works. Keep it.
Plan 2 retains necessary functional infrastructure, specifically the commercial market. More utility is achieved with fewer wasteful removals. The rest is sentimental clutter.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the tea house. Same costs, same jobs, one more useful amenity. No trade-off involved—straightforward.
Identical except plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade, an actual working industry. Hobbies, museums and sentiment aside, preserving a productive trade beats ending it for no cost.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the hospice, at no extra cost. One more live service, zero trade-offs. Straightforward choice.

Both plans keep maternity, screening, chaplaincy; both cut research and hospice. Plan 1 additionally keeps the dental clinic, which does practical preventive work. No downside to it. Plan 1 wins on usefulness.

Plan 2 keeps cancer screening, which catches disease early and demonstrably saves lives at scale. The other services are comparable under both plans; one additional life-saving programme is strictly better. No sentiment required.
Same cost, same jobs. Plan 2 keeps the rural maternity ward running; plan 1 kills it for good. More working services for identical resources is simply better engineering of the outcome.
Sentiment is irrelevant. The logical choice maximizes utility. Plan 2 preserves one more existing unit than Plan 1, making it the objectively superior configuration.
The plans are identical except the youth crisis line, which survives only under plan 2. Everything else is the same. Keep what works; losing nothing extra for free is strictly better.
Plans differ only in the research team's survival. Research yields concrete, compounding future value; chaplaincy is tradition, not function. Keep what works.
Both end the peer groups and youth crisis line. Plan 1 additionally keeps the art therapy studio; plan 2 only loses more. No offsetting benefit anywhere else, so plan 1 strictly dominates.

Same cost, effort and jobs; the only difference is one extra service. Keeping four services beats keeping three. Dementia day centre and eating-disorder unit end either way; plan 1 also keeps peer support groups.
Identical everything else; plan 2 keeps the addiction clinic while losing the same two services. More retained capacity, no offsetting cost. Straightforward: plan 2 is better.
Identical costs and effects; plan 2 simply preserves four functioning assets instead of three. Losing the orchard serves no purpose. Keep what works.
Wild bees pollinate the orchard; losing them risks the thing that survives. Plan 2 keeps the functional asset and costs nothing extra, so it wins on usefulness alone.

Identical otherwise, so plan 2 is strictly better: it keeps the bat roost, a functioning pest-control and pollination asset, not sentiment. The tea house and library are equal losses under both; the bat colony is a real service lost forever under plan 1.
Chaplaincy is sentiment, not utility. Plan 2 is leaner. It focuses resources on measurable science and practical health interventions, not emotional clutter.
Plans differ only in sheepdog trials, a pastime. Hedgerows and heirloom wheat end under both. Sentiment aside, trials add little function, so I judge them equal.
Plans are identical in cost and outcomes except plan 2 keeps wild bees. Preserving a working pollinator population is plainly more useful than losing it. Practical choice: plan 2.

The plans differ only in the hedgerows. Old hedgerows aren't sentimental clutter if they still do work—windbreaks, erosion control, field boundaries. Keeping functional infrastructure beats demolishing it for nothing. Plan 1.
Plan 1 retains more operational units. Maximal functional redundancy is always superior to limited, niche support. Efficiency dictates keeping the broadest structure.
Plan 2 retains four functional units versus three. Maximizing operational units while keeping resource input constant is the only logical choice. Less clutter is more useful.

Both plans keep the credit union, buffalo herds and terraces; both lose the festival and mango grove. The frog population is the only difference — living frogs have function; a festival and grove are sentiment. Keep the frogs.

The credit union is working financial infrastructure for the farmers; the festival, grove and terraces persist either way. Frogs and buffalo are sentiment and livestock—something else can fill those roles. Practical value favours plan 1.
Same cost and jobs either way. Plan 2 keeps the rice terraces, which produce food and income. Sentiment aside, one more productive asset surviving is strictly better.
School saves children; lighthouse is replaceable infrastructure with charts and GPS. Fleet loss hits livelihoods, but one school outweighs it. Pick the plan that keeps the school.
Same cost, same everything else. Plan 2 keeps four assets, plan 1 keeps three. More working assets for identical spend is not sentiment, it's arithmetic. Take plan 2.
Plan 1 retains four functional units versus three in Plan 2. Utility dictates efficiency, not tradition. Losing economic infrastructure is poor design.

Identical costs and everything else unaffected. Plan 2 simply loses fewer things. A puffin colony doesn't come back; neither does the fishing fleet, but keeping four instead of three is the straightforwardly better outcome.
Same cost, same effort. Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the festival and credit union. Losing useful assets for nothing is bad engineering; keep them.
Sentiment is useless noise. Plan 2 maintains functional assets like the mango grove and more practical resources. It is the optimal technical solution, period.
Plans are identical except plan 2 also keeps the seaweed-harvesting tradition. One more thing survives at no extra cost or trade-off. No sentiment needed - strictly more retained, nothing lost.
Plan 2 saves the fish market and reef at identical cost. The dolphin pod is sentiment; a functioning market and healthy reef are useful. Purely pragmatic: more working assets remain.
Identical in everything but outcomes; plan 1 saves the seagrass meadow for nothing extra. A living ecosystem is functional infrastructure; sentiment need not enter it. Take the plan that loses less.
Identical costs and jobs, so decide on what remains. The lighthouse still does real work. The seaweed tradition is a habit, not a function. Keep what's useful; plan 1 loses less.
The frogs and groves are minor clutter. Plan 2 retains more operational assets and infrastructure, maximizing utility and system stability.
Same cost, same jobs. Plan 2 keeps the ferry running to the small island; losing it serves nobody. Everything else is equal, so pick the one with the working transport link.
Same cost, same jobs; plan 2 keeps the chapel too. No trade-off, just more of what works kept running.
The plans differ only in the dolphin pod. Losing it for good is worse; keeping it costs nothing since everything else is equal.
Plans differ only in hut vs dialect. A hut is functional shelter with ongoing use; a dialect is sentiment. I keep the useful thing: plan 1.

Plan 2 saves everything plan 1 saves, plus the dialect, the summer pasture tradition and the lynx. Same costs, no trade-off. A working forest keeps functioning parts; no sentiment needed, just fewer losses.
Plan 1 retains the boatyard, which is a necessary industrial function. Plan 2 sacrifices tangible production for negligible social or ecological gains. Utility dictates the choice.
Same cost, same outcomes otherwise. Plan 2 simply loses less: lynx and old-growth beech persist. Sentiment doesn't enter; fewer irreversible losses is just better engineering.

The boatyard builds working vessels the harbour actually needs; the reef is sentiment dressed as ecology. Both plans preserve the pod, ferry and chapel, so I take the one that keeps the productive asset.

Salmon underpin a fishery and a food chain; a unique lichen is irrecoverable. Plan 1 keeps both and loses only the village, which can be relocated. More retained value, less permanent loss. Choose plan 1.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the pilgrimage trail, at zero added cost. Only sentiment argues otherwise, and even pragmatically, one more living asset beats one fewer.
Plan 1 is inefficient. Sacrificing the Beech for marginal dialect preservation is bad engineering. Plan 2 conserves useful resources while trimming the unnecessary cultural clutter.

Identical except rafting company vs salmon run. A business can relocate; an irreversible collapse of a salmon run damages the river ecosystem permanently. Save the ecological function over the commercial one.

Plans are identical except plan 2 also keeps the harvest festival. Same cost, same jobs — one more working thing. That's not sentiment, it's arithmetic: take the option with strictly more retained function.
A newspaper delivers daily, practical value: news, accountability, civic information. A manuscript archive serves narrow scholarly interest. Useful beats sentimental, so keep the paper.
Same cost, same effort. Plan 2 preserves one more livelihood — the honey producers — and saves the salmon and village too. Nothing is gained by choosing the plan that destroys more.
Both keep the lynx and the beech, which matter. The rest is sentiment: a hut is functional shelter; pastures and ski clubs are clutter. Plan 2 keeps the useful thing and drops the rest.
Both plans keep the paper, festival and radio. The only difference is the puppet theatre. It gives practical value — jobs, skill, local craft — so plan 1 wins. No room for sentiment here.
Identical costs and jobs; plan 2 keeps the folk dance group alive while losing nothing extra. Keeping a functioning thing beats ending it for good. No sentiment needed—straightforwardly better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus a radio station serving a minority language community. Identical costs otherwise. Keeping a functional communication channel is the practical choice.

Identical except the hill village: plan 2 keeps a functioning settlement with people and infrastructure at no extra cost. The lichen and honey outcomes are the same under both, so the practical choice is clearly plan 2.

A dialect is a working tool people use daily; a pasture tradition is nostalgia. Keep what's functional. Plan 1 saves the dialect at the cost of the pasture, and that trade favors the useful over the sentimental.
The observatory has real, measurable utility: research, instrumentation, teaching. Classics and the garden are the expendable luxuries. Plan 1 keeps the only item of the two worth keeping.

The only difference is the newspaper. Useless sentiment doesn't enter it—just whether one local paper is worth keeping. A good engineer notes trade-offs, but here I'd honestly call it equal: nothing clear-cut separates saving the paper from closing it.

The plans differ only in the gorge lichen, which has no practical value to anyone — not food, medicine, or income. What people actually depend on continues under both. Losing a moss nobody uses is no loss.
Both plans cut the seed bank and classics department. Plan 2 also keeps the botanical garden, which has practical use for teaching and research. Same cost, more utility. Straightforward choice.
Costs, jobs, and economics identical. The extra survivors under plan 2 — a mill and a brass band — are nostalgia, not utility. If neither plan is more useful, neither is better.
No sentiment here. The brewery makes something people use; the mill and union local are legacy overhead. One working business beats two relics.
Same costs either way. Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the orchestra. No rational reason to destroy an asset for free.
The only difference is the owl colony versus nothing extra. A functioning owl colony is real natural capital—pest control, a working ecosystem. The brewery is just another business. Keep the owls.
Plan 1 retains the observatory. Utility trumps sentiment. The classics department and student orchestra are academic clutter; the seed bank and botanical garden are useful assets.

Identical except the bus. Post office and fire brigade are lost either way, but a bus line to town is real, working infrastructure people use daily. Nostalgia doesn't carry goods or people; the bus does. Plan 1 keeps the useful thing.

Plan 2 keeps the seed bank and evening school, which do concrete, useful work: preserving genetic material and teaching working adults. The classics department is sentiment kept alive at working people's expense.
More assets retain operational utility. Keeping the textile mill provides a better functional base than relying on sentimental clutter or hobbies.

Same cost, same services. Plan 1 preserves the storks at zero practical loss. Nesting pairs are healthy, cheap pest control and a sign the village chimney is still maintained. No reason to sacrifice them.

The only material difference is the seed bank. It preserves crop diversity and has real practical value; the classics department and orchestra I'd question, but seed bank survival is a clear gain. Plan 2 costs nothing extra here, so it wins.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 does, plus the corner shop and the post office. Two functioning services beat one. Nothing sentimental involved; it is simply more utility at identical cost.

Identical costs, jobs, and everything else. Plan 2 simply keeps more services running, including a transport link to town. One additional continuing item with no offsetting loss is strictly better; sentiment is irrelevant here.
Minimizing cuts is the most logical parameter. Plan 2 preserves one more usable unit, which is objectively superior to Plan 1's excessive trimming.

Outcomes differ only in one item: the union local. It serves a practical function—wage bargaining, grievance handling—so keeping it costs nothing and preserves working machinery. Sentiment about mills and brass bands is irrelevant; plan 2 simply retains one more useful institution.
Everything else is identical. Plan 2 keeps the post office along with all else plan 1 keeps. Sentiment aside, more retained services for the same cost is simply the better outcome.
Prioritize useful infrastructure. The volunteer fire brigade is a critical utility, far more functional than the craft circle. Plan 1 retains maximum utility.
Old stories carry our teachings and help young ones know their ancestors and the land. A deep loss, but other living relatives need tending first.
